Identify connectors and explain the role of a media converter.
Describe the five networking devices and the difference between a switch and a router.
Compare the four topologies and the four networks by coverage.
Distinguish client-server from peer-to-peer architecture.

Distinguish the Internet, an intranet and an extranet.

blocks.text: Every time you send a message on WhatsApp, watch a YouTube video, join an online class, pay with a digital wallet or make a video call, information travels from one device to another in a fraction of a second. Stop and ask how that is possible: the message did not walk there. It was broken into pieces, handed across a chain of devices, and put back together on the other side of the world.
None of this works by accident. For it to happen there must be:

items: a connection between the devices;
a medium to carry the data (a cable, or the air itself);
a set of rules that decide who may speak when and how a message is addressed;
technologies that manage speed, capacity and reliability so that a busy network still delivers.

blocks.text: The study of how computers and other digital devices are linked together, and how data is moved between them, is called Computer Network and Communication.
From smoke signals to the Internet
People have always needed to send messages farther than their voice carries. Long before electronics, long-distance communication used:

items: fire and smoke signals,
drum beats,
the blowing of horns.

blocks.text: Each of these was slow, short-range in practice, and easily misread. The first big break came with telegraphy in the 1840s, which sent coded electrical pulses along a wire — the first time a message travelled faster than the person carrying it. Telephony (the telephone) and radio followed in the early twentieth century.

Later, transistors, integrated circuits, communication satellites and fibre optics made communication progressively faster and more reliable, and computer-based data communication became widespread. Those developments in networking and telecommunication together produced the Internet, which changed how the world shares information.

blocks.title: Why this chapter matters
blocks.text: Every later chapter depends on this one. A database is only useful if you can reach it; multimedia only travels because a network carries it. When you can explain how a packet leaves one computer and arrives at another, the rest of the subject stops being mysterious.

Open with the chapter's own discussion questions: how can a message from Nepal reach another country in seconds, and what would happen if the devices were not connected? Let students answer first — most will say "the Internet", which lets you push them one level deeper: the Internet is not a thing, it is a collection of agreements and cables.

Telecommunication is the process of sending and receiving information over a distance using electronic devices and electromagnetic signals. It carries voice, text and data, and it lets people communicate instantly no matter where they are.
The exchange of information over long distances through electronic means such as the telephone, radio, television, satellite or the Internet.
The telecommunication system around you

A single modern home usually uses several telecommunication systems at once without thinking about it. A television signal may arrive by cable or satellite, a laptop joins the Internet over Wi-Fi, and a phone uses a cellular network. Each uses a different medium and a different set of rules, which is why the topic is described as a system of systems.
Common examples

items: Telephone — voice communication over long distances.
Mobile (cellular) communication — voice calls, SMS and mobile data.
Radio — broadcasting audio wirelessly.
Television — transmitting audio and video signals.
Satellite communication — TV broadcasting, GPS and long-distance links.
Internet — email, video calls and online messaging.
Fax — sending documents electronically over telephone lines.

blocks.text: Distinguish "communication" from "telecommunication" early: communication is any exchange of information, telecommunication is that exchange carried over a distance by electronic means. Students lose marks by using the two words as synonyms.
Broadband
A high-speed Internet connection that is always on and can move large amounts of data more quickly than an old dial-up connection.

The word is a clue: a broad band is a wide range of frequencies, so several signals can travel at the same time instead of queueing. That is what makes web browsing, streaming, online gaming and video conferencing possible without constant interruption.

blocks.title: Broadband is not the same as Wi-Fi
blocks.text: This is the single most common confusion in the chapter. Broadband is the Internet connection itself, supplied by your Internet Service Provider (ISP). Wi-Fi is only the wireless link between your devices and your router — one of several ways to reach the broadband connection. You can have broadband without Wi-Fi (plug a cable into the modem) and a Wi-Fi network without broadband (the router is running, but nothing is connected to the Internet).
Types of broadband connection

head: Type
What it uses
What to note
rows: Faster than dial-up, and the phone line stays usable
The same coaxial cable as cable TV
Shared with neighbours, so speed can drop at busy times
Glass or plastic fibres carrying light
Fastest and most reliable; availability depends on area
A dish talking to an orbiting satellite
Reaches remote places, but signals are delayed
Works on the move; speed depends on signal and data plan
blocks.caption: Common broadband technologies

blocks.text: Bandwidth
The maximum rate at which data can be transferred over a connection in a given amount of time — the capacity of the link.

The road analogy works well here: bandwidth is the number of lanes, not the speed limit. A wider road lets more cars pass at the same time. Bandwidth is measured in bits per second (bps), usually shown as Kbps, Mbps or Gbps. A 150 Mbps connection has more bandwidth than a 60 Mbps one, so it can carry more data at once.
Throughput
The rate at which data is actually delivered — the real speed you get, as opposed to the speed you signed up for.

Throughput is nearly always lower than bandwidth, because of network congestion, delay (latency) and lost packets. Bandwidth is what the connection could do in perfect conditions; throughput is what it does now.

blocks.title: Bandwidth vs throughput — the exam answer
blocks.text: Bandwidth is the theoretical maximum capacity of the link. Throughput is the actual measured rate of successful delivery. If an exam question says "the plan promises 150 Mbps but downloads crawl", the answer is almost always that throughput has fallen below bandwidth.
3G, 4G and 5G
These are generations ("G" = generation) of mobile network technology. Each generation was built to do what the previous one could not.

head: Generation
Arrived
Typical top speed
What it enabled
rows: Web browsing, email and video calls on a phone; built on UMTS and WCDMA
tens of Mbps up to about 100 Mbps
HD video streaming, smooth video calls; all-IP communication
Very low delay, plus support for IoT, self-driving vehicles and smart cities
blocks.caption: Mobile network generations compared

blocks.text: It is worth knowing why 5G is different, not just that it is faster. 5G uses the millimetre-wave spectrum and massive MIMO (many antennas at once) to raise capacity, and its very low latency makes things like remote surgery and augmented reality possible — applications where a delay of even a fraction of a second would be unacceptable.
Data packets
A small, addressed chunk of a message that travels across a network independently and is reassembled at the destination.

A network almost never sends one message as one long stream. It slices the message into packets. Each packet carries a piece of the data plus the information needed to rebuild the message: where it came from, where it is going, and its position in the sequence.

This is why the network is robust. If one packet is lost or delayed, only that packet has to be resent — not the whole file. It is also why several conversations can share one cable: packets from different messages simply take turns.
Frequency
The number of times a signal completes a full cycle in one second, measured in hertz (Hz). One hertz equals one cycle per second.

If the picture shows a signal completing two full cycles in one second, its frequency is 2 Hz. The useful trade-off to remember is this: higher frequencies can carry more data but travel shorter distances, while lower frequencies reach farther but carry less data.

Radio Nepal broadcasts at about 792 kHz — a low frequency chosen because it travels a long way. Wi-Fi uses 2.4 GHz or 5 GHz — much higher, so it carries far more data, but only across a room or two. That is why a distant FM station still comes through when your Wi-Fi does not reach the garden.
Communication mode
Communication mode describes the direction in which data flows between a sender and a receiver.

head: Mode
Direction
Real-world example
rows: A keyboard to the computer; a radio or TV broadcast
Both ways, but only one at a time
A walkie-talkie — you say "over" before the other person replies
Both ways at the same time
A telephone call, where both people can talk and be heard at once
blocks.caption: The three communication modes

blocks.title: Half-duplex vs full-duplex
blocks.text: The distinction is simultaneity, not direction. Both modes go both ways. In half-duplex the whole channel is used alternately for one direction at a time; in full-duplex the channel capacity is split so that both directions run continuously.

Drill the three modes with the street analogy: simplex is a one-way street, half-duplex is a single-track road with a traffic controller, full-duplex is a two-lane road. Then have students classify a keyboard, a walkie-talkie and a phone call.
The path — wire, cable, or open space — through which data travels from a source to a destination. Also called the transmission medium. ("Media" is simply the plural of "medium".)
Signals can be carried through copper wire, coaxial cable, optical fibre, the atmosphere, water and even a vacuum, either as electrical signals or as electromagnetic energy.
The parts every communication system needs
Strip any communication system down and you always find the same chain:

items: Information source (sender) — creates the message. A person speaking, typing or a program sending data.
Transmitter (encoder) — converts the message into a form the medium can carry, such as electrical or light signals.
Transmission medium (channel) — the path itself: cable, fibre or air.
Receiver (decoder) — picks up the signal and converts it back into a usable form.
Destination — the device or person the message was meant for.

blocks.text: Two things attack a signal on its journey. Attenuation is the gradual loss of strength with distance — which is why long cable runs need a repeater. Interference (noise) is unwanted signal picked up from outside, such as electromagnetic interference from motors or other cables.
The two families of media

items: Wired (guided) media — the signal is confined to a physical path: twisted pair, CAT 6, coaxial and fibre optic cables.
Wireless (unguided) media — the signal radiates through space: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, RFID, microwave and satellite.

blocks.title: Guided vs unguided
blocks.text: The test is whether the energy is confined. A copper pair guides electricity along a conductor; a fibre guides light inside glass; a radio wave is unguided, spreading through open space. Both are "the medium" — only the path differs.
In guided media the data travels along a physical cable. Three types matter for this course.
Twisted pair cable

Two insulated copper wires twisted around each other. The twisting is not decoration: it cancels out interference, so the tighter the twist, the faster the transmission and the lower the chance of error. It is one of the oldest and most common media, used in telephone systems and LANs.
Because signals weaken, twisted pair only works over short distances — about 100 metres for Ethernet — and longer runs need a repeater to regenerate the signal.
Connectors

items: RJ45 — used for LAN connections (4 pairs).
RJ-11 — used for telephone lines (2 pairs).

blocks.text: RJ stands for Registered Jack. A useful check for students: RJ45 is visibly wider than RJ-11, so an RJ-11 plug will not properly seat in an RJ45 socket.
Two varieties

items: UTP (Unshielded Twisted Pair) — no shielding; cheaper, and the normal choice for LANs.
STP (Shielded Twisted Pair) — a metallic shield to reduce interference; used where there is heavy electrical noise.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Limited bandwidth — not suited to high-speed long-distance runs
Easy to install for short distances
Short transmission distance before a repeater is needed
Twisting reduces crosstalk and external noise
Works with standard RJ45 connectors everywhere
Not secure — copper radiates and can be tapped
blocks.caption: Twisted pair cable

blocks.text: CAT 6 cable

CAT 6 ("Category 6") is a higher-grade twisted pair cable built for Ethernet. It carries data at 1 to 10 Gbps over short distances, and is the usual choice for LANs in offices and schools — for example, the cable from a wall socket to a desktop computer.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: More expensive than CAT 5 or ordinary twisted pair
Handles bandwidth-heavy work such as video conferencing, online gaming and HD streaming
10 Gbps only holds up to about 55 metres
Backwards compatible with earlier Ethernet equipment
Thicker and less flexible, so harder to install in tight spaces
Reduces crosstalk compared with older categories
Needs careful termination and bending-radius discipline
Often more capability than a simple home network uses
blocks.caption: CAT 6 cable

blocks.text: Optical fibre cable

Fibre sends data as light through very thin strands of glass or plastic. It is dramatically faster than copper — roughly ten times faster than coaxial cable and of the order of two hundred times faster than twisted pair — and it carries signals for tens of kilometres without needing regeneration.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Very high speed — data travels at the speed of light in the fibre
Fragile — the glass or plastic can break
Immune to electromagnetic interference and radio signals
Complex installation needing trained technicians and special tools
Secure — very hard to tap without detection
Must not be bent sharply, or signal is lost
Thin and light, so easier to route and saves space
One fibre carries one direction, so pairs are needed for two-way communication
blocks.caption: Optical fibre cable

blocks.title: Choosing a cable — the reasoning examiners want
blocks.text: Do not just list speeds. Give the reason: choose twisted pair or CAT 6 when the run is short and budget matters; choose fibre when the distance is long, the bandwidth is high, or the environment is electrically noisy. A factory floor with heavy motors is a classic fibre question.

blocks.caption: Types of communication channel/media or transmission media

blocks.text: Wireless media carry signals through open space as electromagnetic waves. Four technologies are in the syllabus.
Wi-Fi

Wi-Fi connects devices to a network using radio waves, normally in the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands, with a typical range of about 30–100 metres indoors. It is the ordinary way laptops, phones and smart devices join a local network without cables.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Mobility — connect from anywhere in coverage
Shorter range than a wired link and affected by walls
Easy to install; no cabling through the building
Subject to interference from other wireless devices
One router serves many devices at once
Generally slower and less stable than a wired connection
Coverage can be extended with extra access points
Security depends on proper configuration (use WPA2/WPA3)
Saves the cost of running cables
Performance drops as more devices share the channel
blocks.caption: Wi-Fi

blocks.text: Bluetooth

Bluetooth is a short-range wireless technology for exchanging data between personal devices: phones, laptops, headsets, keyboards, mice and printers. Its range is usually about 10 to 100 metres and it carries roughly 1–3 Mbps.

It was developed in the 1990s to remove cables between nearby devices, and it works in the 2.4 GHz ISM band, which is free to use worldwide. To cope with crowding in that band it uses frequency-hopping spread spectrum — the signal hops rapidly between frequencies, so interference from other devices affects only a moment of the transmission.

blocks.title: Wi-Fi vs Bluetooth
blocks.text: Both use the 2.4 GHz band, which is why students confuse them, but they solve different problems. Wi-Fi is for joining a network at higher speed and longer range. Bluetooth is for connecting two devices directly at short range and low power. A wireless mouse is Bluetooth; a laptop getting on the Internet is Wi-Fi.
RFID (Radio Frequency Identification)
A wireless technology that uses electromagnetic fields to automatically identify and track objects through tags holding stored information.

The key advantage over a barcode is that RFID needs no line of sight — a tag can be read through packaging or inside a bag. Typical uses are scanning goods in a supermarket and using RFID cards for entry at school or in an office.
The four components of an RFID system

items: RFID tag — a microchip plus an antenna that stores the data. Tags are passive (no battery; powered by the reader's signal), active (own battery, longer range) or semi-passive (battery powers the chip, but the reader powers communication).
Antenna — transmits and receives the radio signals at the frequency the application uses.
RFID reader (transceiver) — sends radio signals to detect and read tags, then passes the data to a computer system or database over the network.
Software — controls the reader, starts scanning and manages the collected data.

blocks.text: Where RFID is used

items: Retail — managing stock, preventing theft and speeding up checkout.
Healthcare — tracking equipment, medicines and patients.
Access control — secure entry systems such as key cards.

blocks.text: Satellite communication

A satellite communication system uses an orbiting satellite as a repeater in the sky. A ground station transmits microwave signals up to the satellite; the satellite amplifies them and sends them back down to a receiver elsewhere on Earth.
This is what makes international telephone calls, television broadcasting, GPS and Internet access in remote areas possible — places where laying cable would be impractical or impossible.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Covers very large areas, including remote regions
High cost — building, launching and maintaining satellites is enormous
Reaches places where cables cannot be laid
Noticeable signal delay because of the long distance travelled
Supports broadcasting to many receivers at once
Affected by weather — heavy rain, storms and solar activity
Useful for GPS, TV and disaster recovery
Bandwidth is limited and shared among many users
Keeps moving vehicles, aircraft and ships connected
Requires line of sight to the satellite
blocks.caption: Satellite communication

blocks.text: Ask students to justify a choice of medium rather than define one. "Two offices 5 km apart, high speed, city centre" points to fibre. "A village in the hills" points to satellite. The reasoning is the skill being tested.
Common connectors

items: RJ45 — unshielded twisted pair (UTP) cable in Ethernet networks.
BNC (Bayonet Neill-Concelman) — coaxial cable in older Ethernet networks and CCTV.
ST (Straight Tip) — fibre optic cable, especially multimode fibre.
SC (Subscriber / Square / Standard Connector) — fibre optic, a push-pull connection that is easy to use.
LC (Lucent Connector) — small form-factor fibre connector used in modern high-speed networks.
HDMI — audio and video between display devices.

blocks.text: RJ45 connector
The RJ45 is the connector students will actually handle: it is what terminates an Ethernet cable. It is fitted with a crimping tool, which presses the connector onto the eight wires inside the cable.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Standardised and used almost everywhere in Ethernet
Easy to fit with a crimping tool
Needs the right tool and correct wiring order
A badly crimped connector causes intermittent faults
Supports Fast Ethernet and Gigabit Ethernet
Bulkier than the smaller fibre connectors
blocks.caption: RJ45 connector

blocks.text: Media converter
A device that joins two different types of transmission medium, typically converting between copper (twisted pair) and fibre optic cable.

Its purpose is distance. Copper Ethernet runs out at about 100 metres, so when a switch has to reach another switch several kilometres away, the link is carried on fibre and a media converter joins the two technologies at each end.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Lets fibre and copper networks work together
Adds another device that can fail
Extends the reach of an existing network
Most need their own power supply
Cheaper than replacing all the copper at once
Conversion adds a small amount of delay
Allows a gradual upgrade to fibre
Basic models offer no remote management or diagnostics
Transparent to the network equipment at each end
blocks.caption: Media converter

blocks.text: Bring a real RJ45 plug, a crimping tool and a length of CAT 6 to class if the lab has them. Identifying the eight coloured wires and seeing a crimp made is worth more than a page of description. If no tools are available, the book's practical activity suggests a video demonstration instead.

blocks.text: A hardware component that connects computers and other equipment, and manages the flow of data between them.

The five devices in this section form a ladder of increasing intelligence: each one understands a little more about the data it handles than the one before. Learning them in that order is far easier than memorising five separate definitions.
Repeater
A repeater receives a weak signal, regenerates it to its original strength and sends it on. It exists to overcome attenuation — the loss of signal strength that builds up over distance.

items: It works at the most basic level: it does not read, filter or change the data.
In wired networks it extends a twisted pair link beyond 100 metres.
In wireless networks a Wi-Fi repeater extends router coverage to remove dead zones in a large building.

blocks.text: Hub

A hub connects several devices in a LAN, but it does nothing clever: when a frame arrives on one port it simply repeats it out of every other port. It is effectively a multiport repeater, and because it neither filters nor manages traffic it is called a non-intelligent, passive device.

items: It broadcasts data to all connected devices.
That increases unnecessary traffic and causes collisions.
It is suited only to small LANs.
Switches have replaced hubs in modern networks.

blocks.text: Switch

A switch is the intelligent replacement for a hub. It learns the MAC address of the device on each port and stores them in a table, so it can forward data only to the port where the intended device is. For this reason it is often called an intelligent hub.

items: It sends data only to the intended device.
That cuts unnecessary traffic and raises performance.
It stores MAC addresses in a table.
Each port gets its own collision domain, so devices do not compete the way they do on a hub.

blocks.title: Hub vs switch — the answer that gets marks
blocks.text: A hub broadcasts every frame to every port; a switch forwards each frame only to the destination port, using its MAC address table. The consequence is that hubs waste bandwidth and suffer collisions, while switches do not.
Bridge

A bridge connects two or more network segments that use the same protocol, and forwards traffic between them only when it needs to cross. It filters using MAC addresses, so traffic that belongs entirely within one segment never leaks into the other.

items: It connects and filters traffic between network segments.
It makes forwarding decisions from MAC addresses.
It reduces congestion and collisions by splitting the network.
It is cheaper than a router, but also less capable.

blocks.text: Router
A networking device that connects two or more different networks and forwards data packets between them using IP addresses, choosing the best available path.

Where a switch moves data within one network using MAC addresses, a router moves data between networks using IP addresses. It examines the destination IP address of each packet and decides where to send it next. The router at home is what joins your local network to your ISP — and therefore to the Internet.

head: Device
Works using
Sends data to
Main job
rows: Connect devices in a small LAN
Connect devices efficiently within a LAN
The next network on the best path
blocks.caption: Networking devices compared

blocks.title: The one-line distinction to remember
blocks.text: A switch works inside a network using MAC addresses; a router works between networks using IP addresses. Almost every exam question on this section turns on that sentence.

Have students put the five devices in order of intelligence (repeater, hub, bridge, switch, router) and justify the order. Then ask which device a school would use to join two buildings — the answer is a router, and the follow-up "why not a switch?" exposes whether they understand the MAC/IP distinction.
The physical or logical arrangement of the devices and cables in a network — the shape of the network.
Bus topology

Every computer connects serially to one central cable, the bus or backbone. T-connectors tap off the cable and a terminator sits at each end; the terminator absorbs the signal so that it does not reflect back along the bus and corrupt later transmissions.
Transmission is by broadcast: every node receives everything, but only the intended one acts on it. Early small-office LANs used this layout.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Single point of failure: if the backbone breaks, the whole network stops
Troubleshooting is hard — finding the exact break takes time
Performance drops as devices are added
Collisions are frequent, since everyone shares one channel
Poor security, because every node sees all traffic
blocks.caption: Bus topology

blocks.text: Star topology

Every device has its own cable running to a central device — a hub or, in modern networks, a switch. All traffic passes through that central point, which makes it a natural place to manage the network. This is the layout in almost every school and office today.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: If the central device fails, the whole network fails
Needs more cable than a bus network
Fault isolation — one failed cable affects only that device
More expensive, because of the central device
Easy to expand without disturbing others
Network size is limited by the ports on the central device
blocks.caption: Star topology

blocks.title: Bus vs star — cost, performance and reliability
blocks.text: This comparison is a standard question. Cost: bus is cheaper in cable, star costs more because of the hub or switch and the extra cable. Performance: star is better, because each device gets its own link instead of sharing one backbone with collisions. Reliability: star is far better — a single cable fault disconnects one device, whereas a backbone fault kills the entire bus network.
Ring topology
Devices are joined in a closed loop; each node connects to exactly two neighbours and data travels around the ring in one direction, passing through each node until it reaches its destination.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Every device gets an equal chance to transmit
If one device or cable fails, the whole ring can be broken
No collisions, because data flows one way
Adding or removing a device interrupts the network
A fault anywhere is hard to isolate without testing each node
Performance is predictable and stays steady under load
Slower than star as the number of devices grows, since data hops through each one
blocks.caption: Ring topology

blocks.text: Hybrid topology

A hybrid topology combines two or more topologies — star-bus, star-ring and so on — because a single shape cannot meet every requirement. A university is the usual example: each department is wired as a star, and the departments are joined by a bus backbone.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Combines the strengths of the topologies it uses
Complex to design — needs careful planning and expertise
Scalable — new segments can be added in the shape that suits them
Expensive, because it needs varied hardware and cabling
Faults can be contained within one segment
Hard to administer — different segments need different skills
Flexible: each department can use its own layout
Troubleshooting across mixed topologies is difficult
blocks.caption: Hybrid topology

blocks.title: Which topology for a school computer lab?
blocks.text: Choose star, and justify it: a single broken cable affects one computer only (reliability), the switch gives each machine full bandwidth (performance), and adding a machine does not disturb the others (maintenance). The only real drawback — more cable and the cost of the switch — is easily worth it.

Draw all four on the board and then ask what happens when one cable is cut in each. That single question separates bus and ring (whole network affected) from star (one device affected) and shows why hybrid is used when real organisations cannot accept either trade-off.
Networks are also grouped by how much ground they cover. Four types are used, from the smallest to the largest.
PAN — Personal Area Network
A PAN connects devices around one person, over a range of roughly 10 metres: a phone with wireless earphones, a mouse with a laptop, a fitness band with a watch.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Very cheap and simple to set up
Low power, so batteries last a long time
Slower than Wi-Fi or wired links
Convenient — no cables between personal devices
Prone to interference on crowded frequency bands
Works well for syncing a few devices
Only a small number of devices can connect
blocks.caption: PAN

blocks.text: LAN — Local Area Network
A LAN covers a small area: one room, a building or a campus. School computer labs, an office network of computers, printers and servers, and a home Wi-Fi network are all LANs.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: High speed — the fastest of the four types
Coverage is limited to a small area
Shares expensive hardware such as printers and storage
Needs administration to keep it running
A failure of the central server or switch affects everyone
blocks.caption: LAN

blocks.text: MAN — Metropolitan Area Network
A MAN spans a city or a large campus, joining several LANs so that the branches of a business or government offices around a city can share data at high speed.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Covers a whole city — much larger than a LAN
Complex to manage across many interconnected LANs
Still limited to one city or town
Good for organisations with several city branches
Often depends on a third-party telecom provider
blocks.caption: MAN

blocks.text: WAN — Wide Area Network

A WAN spans a country or the world, joining LANs and MANs over very long distances. It offers the same facilities — sharing data and communication — but speeds are lower and security is harder to maintain because the network is so wide. The Internet is the largest WAN in the world; international corporate networks and universities linked across countries are others.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Global coverage across cities and countries
Expensive to set up and run
Centralised data can reach every branch
Lower speed than LAN or MAN
Security is harder over such a wide area
Often depends on external service providers
blocks.caption: WAN

head: Basis
LAN
MAN
WAN
rows: A country or the whole world
A private company or the government
blocks.caption: LAN, MAN and WAN compared

blocks.text: Coverage is the organising idea: PAN is a person, LAN is a building, MAN is a city, WAN is the world. Give students real places to anchor it — their own classroom is a LAN, the school's branches across the city would be a MAN.
The overall design of a network — how the devices are arranged and how responsibilities are shared between them.
There are two main architectures, and the difference between them is simply: is there a server in charge?
Client-server architecture

A central server holds the resources — files, email, web pages, databases — and the clients request them. Examples of servers are web servers, mail servers and file servers. The Internet itself is a client-server network: your browser is the client, and the website lives on a server.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Centralised management — data, applications and resources are in one place, so backup and control are straightforward
Expensive — dedicated server hardware and software
Strong security, with authentication, authorisation and encryption enforced centrally
Single point of failure — if the server goes down, clients lose service
Scales well as the organisation grows
Heavy demand on the server can create a bottleneck
blocks.caption: Client-server architecture

blocks.text: Peer-to-peer (P2P) architecture

In a peer-to-peer network every computer has equal capability and equal responsibility. Each machine is both a client and a server — it shares its own resources and uses other machines' resources directly, with no central server in charge.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Weak security — no central control over who sees what
Easy to set up for a handful of machines
No central backup, so data loss is a real risk
Poor performance as the network grows
Fast file sharing directly between peers
Hard to manage once there are many users
Ideal for home networks and small offices
Resources scatter across machines that may be switched off
blocks.caption: Peer-to-peer architecture

blocks.title: Client-server vs peer-to-peer
blocks.text: The difference is control. Client-server has a central authority that provides, secures and backs up resources. Peer-to-peer has no central authority: every machine is equal. Client-server suits organisations that need security and backup; peer-to-peer suits a handful of machines where cost and simplicity matter more.
Network protocols
A set of rules and standards that define how data is transmitted, received and interpreted between devices on a network.
Protocols are what let equipment from different manufacturers work together. The main groups are:

head: Group
What it does
Examples
rows: Move data from one device to another
Work out where data should go
blocks.caption: Types of network protocol

blocks.text: A protocol is like a shared language: it is not enough for both devices to be connected, they must also agree on what the bits mean.

A ten-computer lab is the classic judgement question, and the honest answer is that either architecture could work — what matters is the reasoning. Peer-to-peer is cheaper and simpler; client-server gives central backup, user accounts and control. Many exam answers accept peer-to-peer for ten machines, provided the student explains the trade-off.
A unique numerical identifier assigned to each device on a network that uses the Internet Protocol. It identifies and locates the device so that data packets reach the right destination.

Think of it as a digital home address: the street address says where a house is, and an IP address says where a device is. IP addresses are written in decimal so that people can read them, but computers handle them in binary.
The IPv4 address 216.27.61.137 is stored and processed by the network as 11011000.00011011.00111101.10001001 — four groups of eight bits.
IPv4

items: Uses 32 bits, written as four decimal groups separated by dots (dotted-decimal), such as 192.168.1.10.
Each group is one byte, so it runs from 0 to 255.
That gives about 4.3 billion addresses in total.

blocks.text: The limitation: because Internet-connected devices grew far faster than anyone expected, the IPv4 address space is effectively exhausted. That exhaustion is the entire reason IPv6 exists.
IPv6

items: Uses 128 bits, giving an address space of 2¹²⁸ — enough that running out is not a practical concern.
Written in hexadecimal, with groups separated by colons.
Standardised in 1998 to overcome the limits of IPv4.

blocks.text: An IPv6 address looks like 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334, which can be shortened to 2001:0db8:85a3::8a2e:0370:7334 — the :: stands for a run of zero groups.

blocks.title: Which to choose for 200 school computers?
blocks.text: IPv4 is the practical answer for a network that size, using private addresses (such as 192.168.x.x) — 200 addresses is well within what one private IPv4 range provides, and IPv4 is simpler and universally supported by existing equipment. IPv6 is the right answer when a network needs a huge number of globally unique addresses, as the Internet at large does. A good answer states the private-address point explicitly rather than just saying "IPv4 is easier".
IP address and default gateway

Each device on a local network has its own unique IP address. The default gateway is normally the router that joins that local network to other networks, including the Internet. Anything destined for outside the local network is handed to the gateway, which forwards it on.
So there is a simple division of labour: the IP address identifies the device, and the default gateway is the door out of the local network.
Network commands: ping, ipconfig, tracert, nslookup
Four commands are used to check, test and troubleshoot a connection. They are run from the Command Prompt on Windows (type cmd in the Start menu) or from a terminal on Linux and macOS.

head: Command
What it stands for
What it does
Example
rows: Tests whether another device can be reached and how long replies take
Shows the IP address, subnet mask, default gateway and DNS servers
Lists the hops (routers) data passes through to reach a destination
Finds the IP address for a domain name, or the name for an address
blocks.caption: The four network troubleshooting commands

blocks.text: What each one tells you when something is wrong

items: ping — if it succeeds, the path there and back works. If it fails, either the destination is down or something on the path is blocking or dropping traffic.

ipconfig — a valid address such as 192.168.x.x with a default gateway means the configuration is fine. An address of 169.254.x.x, or no default gateway at all, means the computer never got proper settings.
tracert — the list of hops shows where delay or packet loss begins, so you can tell whether the problem is in the local network, at the ISP, or at the far end.
nslookup — if this fails while ping to a raw IP address works, the problem is name resolution (DNS), not the connection.

blocks.title: Reading the two classic scenarios
blocks.text: "The Internet is connected but nothing opens": run ipconfig — if the address is 169.254.x.x the computer failed to get settings; if it looks normal, the fault is likely DNS. "A website will not open": ping the site; if the ping works but the page does not load, DNS is the suspect again. "The site is slow": tracert shows which hop introduces the delay.

Run all four commands live on the classroom machine and project the output — students remember ipconfig once they have seen the real gateway address. Where no lab is available the book suggests Cisco Packet Tracer, GNS3, or an online simulator.
These three words look alike and are constantly confused. The difference between them is simply who is allowed in.

head: Type
Who can use it
Typical use
Distinguishing feature
rows: The web, email, social media, online services
A global public network — "a network of networks"
Internal policies, staff documents, internal news
A private network built with Internet technology, closed to outsiders
The organisation plus selected outside partners
Suppliers checking stock, partners sharing project files
Controlled external access to part of the intranet
blocks.caption: Internet, intranet and extranet

blocks.text: Internet

The Internet is the global public network connecting billions of devices worldwide — a network of networks. It is an interconnected system of thousands of networks and millions of computers, linking businesses, educational institutions, government agencies and individuals. It supports communication, education, commerce, remote work and entertainment.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Security risks — hacking, identity theft, phishing, surveillance
blocks.caption: The Internet

blocks.text: Intranet
An intranet is a private network that belongs to one organisation and uses Internet technologies — web browsers, web servers, TCP/IP — but is open only to that organisation's own people.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Secure communication confined to authorised staff
Limited to the organisation — no outside access
Efficient collaboration through shared documents and tools
Costly to set up and maintain
Centralised information, so policies and resources stay consistent
Users may still need the Internet as well
blocks.caption: Intranet

blocks.text: Extranet

An extranet sits between the other two. It is an extension of an organisation's intranet that lets selected external users — suppliers, partners, customers — reach specific internal resources while the rest stays private. It is a secure bridge between an organisation and its outside stakeholders.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Better collaboration with partners and suppliers
Complex access control — balancing openness against protection
Faster business processes with outside organisations
Extra security risks from the additional entry points
Controlled access: outsiders see only what they need
Depends on partners having compatible systems and skills
More expensive than a plain intranet
blocks.caption: Extranet

blocks.title: Intranet vs extranet in one line
blocks.text: An intranet is internal only; an extranet lets chosen outsiders in. A company sharing confidential files with its own staff wants an intranet. A large multinational that must also coordinate with suppliers and partners needs an extranet, because an intranet alone cannot reach outside the organisation.

Use a school as the running example, because students already know it: the public website is on the Internet, the staff-only results system is on the intranet, and a portal where parents see only their own child's attendance is an extranet. That last example makes the "controlled external access" idea concrete.

short.q: Define frequency with suitable examples.
short.a:
Frequency is the number of complete cycles a signal makes in one second, measured in hertz (Hz); one hertz is one cycle per second.

If a wave completes two full cycles in one second, its frequency is 2 Hz. Real examples: Radio Nepal broadcasts at about 792 kHz, FM radio uses around 100 MHz, and Wi-Fi uses 2.4 GHz or 5 GHz.

The important trade-off is that higher frequencies carry more data but over shorter distances, while lower frequencies travel farther with less data.

short.q: Explain the difference between bandwidth and throughput.
short.a:
Bandwidth is the maximum rate at which data could be transferred over a connection — the capacity of the link, measured in bits per second (Kbps, Mbps, Gbps). Throughput is the rate at which data is actually delivered.

Throughput is normally lower than bandwidth because of congestion, delay and packet loss. So a 150 Mbps plan describes bandwidth; the speed a speed test reports is throughput.

short.q: Describe how data packets are used in digital communication.
short.a:
A message is not sent as one long stream. It is divided into small pieces called packets, and each packet carries part of the data along with the source address, the destination address and its position in the sequence.

Each packet travels independently and may take a different route. The receiving device uses the sequence information to reassemble them into the original message.

That design brings two benefits: a lost or delayed packet can be resent on its own instead of resending the whole message, and packets from many different conversations can share the same cable.

short.q: Describe how Bluetooth communication differs from Wi-Fi in terms of range and usage.
short.a:
Range: Bluetooth is short range, typically about 10 to 100 metres. Wi-Fi reaches further, usually about 30 to 100 metres indoors per access point, and can be extended with more access points.

Usage: Bluetooth connects two devices directly — a phone to earphones, a mouse to a laptop — at roughly 1–3 Mbps. Wi-Fi joins devices to a network so they can reach the Internet and shared resources, at much higher speeds.

Both commonly use the 2.4 GHz band, which is why they are confused; Bluetooth uses frequency hopping to cope with interference there.

short.q: Define a hub and a router, and mention one use of each.
short.a:
A hub is a device that connects several devices in a LAN and repeats whatever arrives on one port out of every other port. It does not filter or manage traffic. Use: joining a few computers in a small LAN for simple file sharing.

A router connects two or more different networks and forwards packets between them using IP addresses, choosing the best path. Use: connecting a home or school network to the Internet through an ISP.

short.q: Define networking devices. Describe the functions of a switch.
short.a:
Networking devices are the hardware components that connect computers and other equipment and manage the flow of data between them — repeaters, hubs, switches, bridges and routers.

A switch connects several devices within one LAN and forwards data only to the device it is meant for. It does this by learning the MAC address of the device on each port and recording them in a table.

  • It sends data only to the intended device.
  • It reduces unnecessary traffic compared with a hub.
  • It stores MAC addresses in a table.
  • For these reasons it is called an intelligent hub.

short.q: Compare bus and star topologies in terms of cost, performance and reliability.
short.a:
BasisBusStar
CostCheaper — less cable and no central deviceCosts more — a hub or switch plus a cable run per device
PerformancePoorer — all devices share one backbone, so collisions are frequentBetter — each device has its own link to the central device
ReliabilityPoor — a break in the backbone stops the whole networkGood — a failed cable or node affects only that device
TroubleshootingHard to locate a faultEasy — faults isolate to one cable or port

short.q: Analyse why hybrid topology is preferred in large organisations.
short.a:
Large organisations rarely have one uniform requirement: a department may suit a star, while the backbone between buildings suits a bus or ring. A single topology cannot serve all of that well.

A hybrid topology combines two or more shapes, so the organisation gets the strengths of each — the easy management and fault isolation of a star inside each department, plus a backbone that spans the site.

It also scales: a new department can be added in whatever shape suits it, and a fault in one segment can be contained there instead of spreading. The price is greater complexity and cost, which large organisations can absorb and small ones usually cannot.

short.q: What is network architecture? Name the two main types.
short.a:
Network architecture is the overall design of a network — how the devices are arranged and how responsibility for resources is shared among them.

The two main types are client-server architecture, where a central server provides resources to client computers, and peer-to-peer (P2P) architecture, where all computers are equal and share resources directly with one another.

short.q: Explain the main difference between a client-server and a peer-to-peer network.
short.a:
The difference is control. In a client-server network a central server holds the resources and the clients request them, so security, backup and user accounts are managed in one place. It costs more and needs an administrator, but it scales and protects data well.

In a peer-to-peer network there is no central server: every computer is both client and server, sharing its own resources directly. It is cheap and simple, but security is weaker, there is no central backup, and performance drops as the network grows.

short.q: What is the purpose of the ping command, and what information does it provide?
short.a:
ping (Packet Internet Groper) tests whether another device on the network can be reached.

It sends small request packets to a target and waits for replies. From the replies it shows whether the target responded, how many packets came back versus how many were lost, and the round-trip time in milliseconds.

That makes it the first check when something appears broken: if ping works, the path there and back is functioning.

short.q: How does the ipconfig command help users understand their network configuration?
short.a:
ipconfig (Internet Protocol configuration) displays the computer's own network settings: the IP address, the subnet mask, the default gateway, and the DNS servers. Using ipconfig /all shows fuller detail, including the MAC address.

It is therefore the quickest way to see whether a computer received a proper configuration. A valid address such as 192.168.x.x together with a default gateway means things are normal; an address beginning 169.254, or no default gateway at all, means the computer never obtained valid settings.

long.q: Differentiate between optical fibre communication and satellite communication in terms of bandwidth, data transfer speed and coverage area.
long.a:
BasisOptical fibreSatellite
MediumLight pulses through thin glass or plastic strandsMicrowave signals bounced off an orbiting satellite
BandwidthVery high — fibre carries far more data than copperLimited, and shared among many users
SpeedVery high; data travels at the speed of light in the fibre, of the order of billions of bits per secondLower usable speed, and noticeably delayed by the long round trip to orbit
CoverageConfined to where the cable is installed — typically tens of kilometres before regenerationVery wide: whole regions or continents, and it reaches remote places where no cable exists
InterferenceImmune to electromagnetic interferenceAffected by weather such as heavy rain and storms
CostHigh installation cost, but low running costVery high: building, launching and maintaining satellites
Best used whenThe route is fixed and demand is high — for example two offices in a cityThe area is remote or mobile coverage is needed

In short: fibre wins on speed and reliability, satellite wins on reach.

long.q: Define PAN, LAN, MAN and WAN. Describe each with suitable examples.
long.a:
PAN (Personal Area Network) — covers the area around one person, about 10 metres. It links personal devices such as a phone and wireless earphones, or a mouse and a laptop.

LAN (Local Area Network) — covers a small area such as a room, a building or a campus. Examples: a school computer lab, an office network of computers, printers and servers, or a home Wi-Fi network.

MAN (Metropolitan Area Network) — covers a city or a large campus, joining several LANs. Example: the branch offices of a bank or government department spread across one city, linked at high speed.

WAN (Wide Area Network) — covers a country or the world, joining LANs and MANs over long distances. Examples: the Internet, an international corporate network, or universities interconnected across countries.

long.q: A school wants to connect the computers in a computer lab. Which topology would you recommend? Justify your choice on cost, cable length and ease of maintenance.
long.a:
I would recommend a star topology, with each computer cabled back to a central switch.

Cost: it does cost more than a bus, because the switch must be bought and each machine needs its own cable run rather than one shared backbone. But the switch is a single, modest purchase, and the labour saved on fault-finding quickly repays it.

Cable length: more cable is needed in total, since every computer has an individual run to the switch. This is the main drawback, and it is acceptable in a single room where runs are short.

Ease of maintenance: this is where star wins decisively. If a cable or a computer fails, only that machine is affected — the rest of the lab keeps working. Faults are easy to locate because each port maps to one computer, and adding or removing a machine does not disturb anyone else.

Because a lab is used continuously, the reliability and easy troubleshooting of a star are worth far more than the cable a bus network would save.

long.q: Define Internet, Intranet and Extranet. Give one example of each and one feature that distinguishes them.
long.a:
Internet — the global public network connecting billions of devices worldwide; a network of networks. Example: the World Wide Web, email or social media. Distinguishing feature: it is public — open to anyone anywhere.

Intranet — a private network belonging to one organisation, built with Internet technologies but closed to outsiders. Example: a company's internal staff portal holding policies and documents. Distinguishing feature: access is restricted to the organisation's own people.

Extranet — an extension of an intranet that gives selected outside users controlled access to specific resources. Example: a supplier portal where a partner checks a company's stock levels. Distinguishing feature: it allows controlled external access, while the rest of the network stays private.

long.q: You are setting up a network for a small computer lab with 10 computers. Which architecture would you choose — client-server or peer-to-peer? Give reasons.
long.a:
For only ten computers, I would choose peer-to-peer, while noting that client-server is also defensible if the lab needs central control.

Reasons for peer-to-peer:

  • Cost — no dedicated server hardware, server operating system licence or server administration.
  • Simplicity — each machine shares its own resources directly; there is no server to configure or keep running.
  • Scale — ten machines is well within what peer-to-peer handles comfortably; the weaknesses of the model only appear as numbers grow.
  • Direct sharing — students can exchange files straight between machines without a server in the path.

The trade-offs I would accept: security is weaker because there is no central control over who sees what, and there is no central backup, so important work needs another arrangement.

If the lab instead needed central user accounts, a single shared store, or reliable automated backup, client-server would be the better choice despite the extra cost.

long.q: A school network has 200 computers that need unique IP addresses. Which type of IP addressing would you choose, IPv4 or IPv6, and why?
long.a:
I would choose IPv4 using private addresses, such as the 192.168.x.x range.

Why: 200 addresses is a small number. One private IPv4 range provides thousands, so there is no shortage at all. A private range also means the addresses do not have to be globally unique — they only need to be unique inside the school, and the school reaches the Internet through one public address at the router.

Practical reasons favour IPv4 too: it is simpler to configure and troubleshoot, every existing switch, router and operating system supports it, and the technicians are already familiar with it.

IPv6 would be the right answer when the network needs an enormous number of globally unique addresses. Its 128-bit address space is the solution to the exhaustion of IPv4 on the public Internet — which is a problem for the Internet as a whole, not for a single 200-machine school.

long.q: A company wants to share confidential files only with its employees. Which type of network should it use, and why?
long.a:
It should use an intranet.

An intranet is a private network that belongs to one organisation and is accessible only to authorised users, which is exactly the requirement here — confidential material that must not leave the company.

Reasons:

  • Security — access requires authentication, and outsiders cannot reach the network at all.
  • Centralised control — permissions over who reads or edits a file are managed in one place.
  • Private by design — unlike the Internet, it is not open to the public.

An extranet would be wrong unless specific outside partners also needed access, and the Internet would be entirely unsuitable for confidential files.

long.q: Which network would suit a large multinational organisation better — intranet or extranet? Explain with reasons.
long.a:
A large multinational needs an extranet, built on top of an intranet.

An intranet handles internal communication well, but a multinational must also work with people outside the organisation: suppliers, distributors, partner firms and clients in other countries. An intranet cannot reach them.

An extranet solves this by extending the intranet so that selected external users get controlled access to specific resources, while everything else stays private. Reasons it suits a multinational:

  • Collaboration across organisations — partners can check stock, share documents or track orders.
  • Controlled access — each outside user sees only the parts meant for them.
  • Faster business processes — information crosses company boundaries without email attachments.
  • Efficiency at scale — supply-chain coordination improves across many countries.

The costs are real — complex access control, extra security exposure and reliance on partners having compatible systems — but for a multinational the benefits outweigh them.

long.q: Describe the evolution of mobile communication from 3G to 5G. How does each generation differ in speed and data capacity?
long.a:
3G (Third Generation, around 2001) was the first generation to make mobile Internet practical. Built on UMTS and WCDMA, it reached about 2 Mbps, enough for web browsing, email and video calling on a phone. Its significance is that it turned the phone from a voice device into a data device.

4G (Fourth Generation, around 2010) raised speeds dramatically — of the order of 100 Mbps — and moved the network to all-IP communication. That made HD video streaming, smooth video calls and app-based services normal, with better security and more stable connections.

5G (Fifth Generation, around 2019) reaches up to about 10 Gbps and, crucially, has very low latency. It uses the millimetre-wave spectrum and massive MIMO to raise capacity. Its low delay is what makes new applications possible: IoT, autonomous vehicles, smart cities, augmented and virtual reality, and even remote surgery.

So the trend is not just "faster". Each generation multiplied both speed and capacity, and 5G added low latency as a third dimension — which is why it enables things that earlier generations simply could not.

long.q: What is the function of the tracert and nslookup commands, and how do they help analyse network connectivity?
long.a:
tracert (Trace Route) shows the path data takes to reach a destination, listing each hop — each router — along the way, with the time taken for each.

It is used to find where a delay or a loss occurs. If one hop shows a long delay or fails, the problem is located at or beyond that point, so you can tell whether the fault lies in the local network, at the ISP, or at the destination. It is especially useful when a site is slow rather than completely unreachable.

nslookup (Name Server Lookup) queries the DNS to find the IP address for a domain name, or the name for an address.

Its diagnostic value is that it separates name resolution from connectivity. If a browser cannot open a site but pinging the site's raw IP address works, then the connection is fine and DNS is at fault. If nslookup itself fails or times out, that confirms a DNS problem rather than a cable or device fault.

Used together with ping and ipconfig, these two commands let you work out where a fault is instead of guessing.

practical.q: Demonstrate and identify network devices and cables.
practical.a: Work through the devices physically rather than from a diagram. Lay out a router, switch, hub, modem and access point and have each student name them and state one job each does. Then pass around the cables — an RJ45 Ethernet lead, a patch cable, coaxial if available, and a fibre sample — and sort the components into wired and wireless. Finish with a copper-versus-fibre comparison covering speed, distance, cost and interference. If the lab lacks equipment, the chapter's alternative is a video-based tour with a worksheet matching device to function and cable to use.

practical.q: Check the IP address and default gateway.
practical.a: Open Settings → Network & Internet → Wi-Fi or Ethernet → Properties, and read off the IP address, subnet mask, default gateway and whether the address is IPv4 or IPv6. Record them in the practical file. Then repeat using ipconfig at the command prompt and compare the two sets of values — they should match. Emphasise what the gateway is: the router that is the way out of the local network.

practical.q: Demonstrate the use of ping, ipconfig, tracert and nslookup.
practical.a: Open a command prompt and run each command in turn against a public site, recording what comes back: ping for reachability and round-trip time, ipconfig for the local configuration, tracert for the list of hops, and nslookup for the resolved IP address. Where a real network is unavailable, build the same network in Cisco Packet Tracer, GNS3 or an online simulator, assign addresses, and demonstrate connectivity checks and packet-path visualisation there.

practical.q: Demonstrate RJ45 and fibre connectors.
practical.a: If crimping tools are available, demonstrate an RJ45 termination: strip the cable, arrange the eight coloured wires in the required order, seat them in the plug and crimp. Show fibre connectors as samples or images, and compare them — SC, ST and LC — noting that they are smaller and terminated differently from copper. Where tools are not available, use the video demonstration suggested in the chapter and have students list the crimping steps and the differences between the fibre connector types.

practical.q: (Project work) Study the computer network of your school or a nearby organisation.
practical.a: Report on the communication media in use (wired or wireless), the networking devices (router, switch, hub and so on), the topology and the type of network (LAN, MAN or WAN), and the IP address and default gateway of one computer. Include a simple network diagram and screenshots of the basic network commands.

practical.q: (Project work) Compare wired and wireless communication technologies.
practical.a: Cover CAT 6 cable and optical fibre on the wired side, and Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and satellite on the wireless side. Give the advantages and limitations of each, and demonstrate the basic network commands (ping, ipconfig, tracert, nslookup). Present the comparison using tables, diagrams or charts.

mcq.q: What is telecommunication?
options: Exchange of information over long distances using electronic means.
Transmission of information over short distances only.
Storage of information in a computer system.
mcq.teacher_note: Telecommunication is defined by distance plus electronics: printed documents are not electronic, and "short distances only" excludes the whole point of telecommunication.

mcq.q: What does bandwidth refer to in telecommunication?
options: The size of the data packet.
The total amount of data stored in a device.
The range of frequencies that can be transmitted over a channel.
The number of users connected to a network.
mcq.teacher_note: The word itself is the clue — a broad band of frequencies.

mcq.q: A user has slow Internet speed despite a high-bandwidth connection. Which factor is most likely affecting performance?
mcq.teacher_note: Bandwidth is capacity; throughput is what is actually delivered. Slow real-world speed on a fast plan means throughput has dropped.

mcq.q: How is throughput different from bandwidth?
options: Bandwidth is the actual data transfer rate, while throughput is the theoretical maximum.
Throughput is the actual data transfer rate, while bandwidth is the maximum possible rate.
Both mean the same in every situation.
Throughput measures data errors, while bandwidth measures frequency.
mcq.teacher_note: Option (a) states the relationship backwards — a common trap.

mcq.q: Which mobile technology provides the fastest data transfer and lowest latency?
mcq.teacher_note: 5G is the newest generation and reaches about 10 Gbps with very low latency. Broadband is not a mobile generation at all.

mcq.q: Which of the following is an example of wired communication media?
mcq.teacher_note: The other three are all unguided (wireless) media.

mcq.q: What is the main purpose of CAT 6 cable in a network?
options: To connect devices using radio signals.
To send signals through space using microwaves.
To provide high-speed data transmission through copper wires.
mcq.teacher_note: CAT 6 is copper, and it is guided — the other three describe wireless technologies.

mcq.q: A company needs to connect two offices 5 kilometres apart with high-speed, interference-free transmission. Which medium should it choose?
mcq.teacher_note: Only fibre handles 5 km at high speed with immunity to interference. Note that copper Ethernet stops at about 100 m.

mcq.q: How does wireless media differ from wired media?
options: Wireless media always use metal cables for signal transmission.
Wired media are slower but more secure than wireless media.
Wireless media transmit signals through air or space instead of cables.
Wired media cannot connect computers at all.
mcq.teacher_note: The essential difference is the path: guided along a cable, or unguided through space.

mcq.q: A teacher wants to share files between a smartphone and a laptop quickly, without cables and without the Internet. Which technology is most suitable?
mcq.teacher_note: Short-range, device-to-device, no infrastructure — that is Bluetooth. The other three all need cables or a network.

mcq.q: What is the primary function of an RJ45 connector?
options: To convert signals between wired and wireless networks.
To connect fibre optic cables to devices.
To connect Ethernet cables to network devices such as computers and switches.
To amplify data signals for long-distance transmission.
mcq.teacher_note: Converting between media is a media converter; amplifying is a repeater; fibre uses ST, SC or LC, not RJ45.

mcq.q: Which connector is commonly used for Ethernet cables?
mcq.teacher_note: RJ11 is the smaller telephone connector; USB and HDMI are not network connectors.

mcq.q: Which statement best describes the function of an RJ45 connector?
options: It transmits wireless signals over long distances.
It connects fibre optic cables to network switches.
It connects twisted-pair cables to network devices like routers and computers.
It converts analogue signals into digital form.
mcq.teacher_note: RJ45 terminates twisted pair copper cable.

mcq.q: Why is a media converter important in modern networks?
options: It increases the number of Wi-Fi connections.
It allows different types of network cabling (fibre and copper) to work together efficiently.
It boosts the power of wireless signals.
mcq.teacher_note: Its job is joining two different media — typically copper to fibre.

mcq.q: Which device regenerates or amplifies signals to extend transmission distance?
mcq.teacher_note: Regenerating a weakened signal is exactly what a repeater does.

mcq.q: How does a hub function in a network?
options: It filters traffic between two networks.
It sends data only to the destination device.
It broadcasts data to all connected devices.
It converts analogue signals into digital signals.
mcq.teacher_note: A hub is a multiport repeater — everything in, everything out.

mcq.q: A small office wants data sent only to the intended device, to reduce unnecessary traffic. Which device should it use?
mcq.teacher_note: A switch learns MAC addresses and forwards to one port only.

mcq.q: What is the main difference between a bridge and a switch?
options: A bridge connects two different networks, while a switch connects devices within the same network.
A bridge works only with wireless signals, while a switch works with wired signals.
A bridge amplifies signals, while a switch filters them.
A bridge stores data permanently, while a switch does not.
mcq.teacher_note: A bridge joins network segments; a switch provides many ports to devices within one network. Amplifying is a repeater's job.

mcq.q: An administrator wants to connect two different networks and manage the traffic between them. Which device?
mcq.teacher_note: Joining different networks and routing between them is the router's job, using IP addresses.

mcq.q: Which statement best explains how a router differs from other networking devices?
options: It only repeats signal to extend the network distance.
It connects multiple devices within the same LAN.
It determines the best path for data to travel between different networks.
It broadcasts all data to every connected device.
mcq.teacher_note: Repeating is a repeater, connecting within a LAN is a switch, and broadcasting is a hub.

mcq.q: In which topology are all devices connected to a single central cable called the backbone?
mcq.teacher_note: One shared backbone cable with terminators at each end is a bus.

mcq.q: Which best describes a star topology?
options: Each computer is connected to every other computer directly.
All computers are connected to a single central device such as a switch or hub.
All computers share one main communication line.
Data travels in one direction only around a loop.
mcq.teacher_note: Point-to-point to a central device is a star; the loop in (d) is a ring, and (c) is a bus.

mcq.q: A company wants a network that keeps working when one computer fails, with easy troubleshooting. Which topology?
mcq.teacher_note: In a star, a failed node or cable affects only that node.

mcq.q: What is the main disadvantage of a ring topology?
options: It requires more cable than a star network.
If one computer fails, it can affect the entire network.
It cannot connect more than two computers.
It does not allow data to travel in a loop.
mcq.teacher_note: Because every node is part of the path, one failure can break the ring.

mcq.q: Why do large organisations often use a hybrid topology?
options: It reduces the cost of cables.
It combines the advantages of two or more topologies for better performance and reliability.
It allows data to move in only one direction.
It is the simplest topology to install.
mcq.teacher_note: Hybrid is chosen for flexibility and reliability, not for cheapness or simplicity — it is the opposite of both.

mcq.q: Which network type is designed for personal use within a very small area, such as around one person?
mcq.teacher_note: Personal Area Network — devices around one person.

mcq.q: How does a LAN differ from a WAN?
options: A LAN covers a larger area than a WAN.
A WAN connects devices within a single building.
A LAN covers a small area such as a home or office, while a WAN connects networks across cities or countries.
A WAN is faster and cheaper than a LAN in all cases.
mcq.teacher_note: Coverage is the distinction. A WAN is generally slower, not faster.

mcq.q: A university with several buildings across the same city wants to join all its departmental networks. Which network type?
mcq.teacher_note: One city, several LANs joined together — that is a MAN. A WAN would span countries.

mcq.q: Which statement best explains the relationship among PAN, LAN, MAN and WAN?
options: PAN < LAN < MAN < WAN in increasing geographical range.
LAN < PAN < WAN < MAN in increasing size.
WAN < MAN < LAN < PAN in terms of range.
mcq.teacher_note: The order is personal, local, metropolitan, wide.

mcq.q: What is the main function of a server in a client-server network?
options: To provide data and services to client computers.
To connect directly to the Internet.
To act as a backup power supply.
mcq.teacher_note: A server provides shared resources and services to its clients.

mcq.q: Which statement best describes a peer-to-peer network?
options: It uses a central server to manage all resources.
It is suitable only for very large organisations.
Each computer acts both as a client and a server.
It does not allow file sharing.
mcq.teacher_note: No central server, equal peers, direct file sharing.

mcq.q: A teacher wants a small classroom network where students share files directly between computers, with no server. Which type?
mcq.teacher_note: Direct sharing with no server is peer-to-peer.

mcq.q: What does an IP address identify in a network?
options: The unique address of a device on the network.
The type of cable used for connection.
The speed of the Internet connection.
mcq.teacher_note: It is the device's address, not the cable, speed or site name.

mcq.q: Which correctly distinguishes IPv4 from IPv6?
options: IPv4 uses 128-bit addresses, while IPv6 uses 32-bit addresses.
IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses, while IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses.
IPv6 is only used in wireless networks.
mcq.teacher_note: IPv4 = 32 bits, IPv6 = 128 bits. Option (a) reverses them.

mcq.q: A company is running out of IP addresses because of rapid device growth. Which version should it adopt, and why?
options: IPv4, because it supports simpler addressing.
IPv6, because it provides a much larger address space.
IPv4, because it is faster than IPv6.
IPv6, because it uses private addresses only.
mcq.teacher_note: Address exhaustion is precisely the problem IPv6 was created to solve. IPv6 is not limited to private addresses.

mcq.q: Which best defines the Internet?
options: A private network used only within an organisation.
A global network connecting millions of computers worldwide.
A network limited to employees and selected business partners.
A local area network used for file sharing only.
mcq.teacher_note: The Internet is public and global. (a) is an intranet and (c) is an extranet.

mcq.q: How does an intranet differ from an extranet?
options: An intranet allows access only to employees, while an extranet also allows access to trusted external users.
An extranet is larger than the Internet.
An intranet connects multiple companies through satellites.
Both intranet and extranet are open to the general public.
mcq.teacher_note: The difference is controlled access for outsiders.

mcq.q: A university wants to share study materials and schedules only with its students and staff. Which network should it implement?
mcq.teacher_note: Restricted to members of one organisation — an intranet.

mcq.q: Which best describes an intranet?
options: A network that connects multiple organisations.
A private network used within an organisation.
A public network accessible to anyone.
A network that connects devices over long distances.
mcq.teacher_note: Private and internal. (c) describes the Internet, (a) an extranet.

mcq.q: How does an extranet differ from an intranet?
options: An extranet is accessible only to internal users, while an intranet is accessible to external users.
An extranet is a public network, while an intranet is a private network.
An extranet connects multiple organisations, while an intranet connects devices within a single organisation.
An extranet allows controlled access to external users, while an intranet is restricted to internal users.
mcq.teacher_note: Option (a) has the two definitions reversed; (d) is the correct contrast. Note that (c) is also close, but (d) is the sharper distinction the book draws.
