quick_revision.title: Foundations
points: Computer Network and Communication is the study of how devices are connected and how data moves between them.
Telecommunication is the exchange of information over a distance by electronic means.
Every communication system needs a sender, a transmitter, a medium, a receiver and a destination.
Attenuation is loss of strength with distance; interference is unwanted signal picked up from outside.

quick_revision.title: Key terms you must distinguish
points: Broadband is the Internet connection from your ISP; Wi-Fi is only the wireless link to the router.
Bandwidth is the maximum possible rate; throughput is what is actually delivered, and it is always lower.
Frequency is cycles per second in hertz: higher frequency carries more data but over a shorter distance.
3G brought mobile data (about 2 Mbps), 4G brought HD video and all-IP, 5G brings about 10 Gbps and very low latency.

quick_revision.title: Media and connectors
points: Wired (guided): twisted pair, CAT 6, optical fibre. Wireless (unguided): Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, RFID, satellite.
Twisted pair is cheap and short-range; RJ45 for LAN, RJ-11 for telephone. UTP has no shielding, STP does.
Fibre carries light: very fast, long distance, immune to interference, but expensive and fragile.
A media converter joins copper to fibre, extending reach beyond the 100 m limit of copper Ethernet.

quick_revision.title: Devices — the ladder of intelligence
points: Repeater regenerates a weak signal; it does not read the data.
Hub broadcasts to every port — a multiport repeater.
Switch forwards to one port using a MAC address table.
Bridge filters between segments using MAC addresses.
Router joins different networks and routes using IP addresses.
The one-line rule: a switch works inside a network with MAC addresses; a router works between networks with IP addresses.

quick_revision.title: Topologies
points: Bus: one backbone, terminators at both ends, cheap but a single break kills the network.
Star: all devices to a central switch — the modern standard, easy to troubleshoot and expand.
Ring: a closed loop, no collisions, but one failure can break it.
Hybrid: two or more topologies combined — flexible and scalable, but complex and costly.

quick_revision.title: Coverage and architecture
points: PAN (a person) < LAN (a building) < MAN (a city) < WAN (the world).
Client-server: a central server provides resources — secure, backed up, but costly and needs an administrator.
Peer-to-peer: all machines equal, no server — cheap and simple, but weaker security and slower as it grows.
A protocol is the set of rules that lets different equipment communicate.

quick_revision.title: Addressing and commands
points: IPv4 is 32 bits in dotted decimal; IPv6 is 128 bits in hexadecimal. IPv4 exhaustion is why IPv6 exists.
The IP address identifies the device; the default gateway is the way out of the local network.
ping tests reachability, ipconfig shows your own configuration, tracert shows the path, nslookup resolves names to addresses.
An address of 169.254.x.x or no default gateway means the computer never got valid settings.

quick_revision.title: Internet, intranet, extranet
points: Internet: public and global, open to anyone.
Intranet: private, one organisation, internal users only.
Extranet: an intranet extended to give selected outsiders controlled access.
The test is always who is allowed in.

teaching_plan.topic: Introduction and the concept of telecommunication
teaching_plan.activity: Start from the chapter's discussion questions. Draw the chain from smoke signals to telegraphy to the Internet on the board, then define telecommunication and work through its examples.
Use the road analogy throughout (lanes versus actual traffic). Insist on the broadband/Wi-Fi distinction — it is the most common error.

teaching_plan.topic: Mobile generations, data packets and frequency
teaching_plan.activity: Build the 3G/4G/5G comparison table. Demonstrate packets by tearing a page into addressed envelopes, and frequency with a simple drawn wave.

teaching_plan.topic: Communication mode and the communication system
teaching_plan.activity: Cover simplex, half-duplex and full-duplex with the street analogy, then walk through the five parts of a communication system.
Pass round real twisted pair, CAT 6 and a fibre sample if available. Build the advantages/disadvantages table for each cable.
Compare Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, RFID and satellite. Give students scenarios (a village, a warehouse, two offices) and ask them to justify a choice.
Identify connectors from real samples or images. Demonstrate or show a video of RJ45 crimping, and explain why copper-to-fibre conversion is needed.
Present the five devices as a ladder of increasing intelligence. Finish with the switch-versus-router distinction.
Draw all four on the board, then ask what happens when one cable is cut in each. That question carries the whole lesson.
Anchor each type to a real place students know: their desk, the school, the city, the world.
Debate the ten-computer lab question. Emphasise that the reasoning matters more than the choice.
Convert an IPv4 address to binary on the board. Explain private addresses and why 200 machines do not need IPv6.
Run ping, ipconfig, tracert and nslookup live and project the output. Work through the two troubleshooting scenarios.
Use the school as the running example: public website, staff-only system, parent portal. Then begin the exercise.

blocks.text: Every day we deal with large amounts of information. A school keeps student records, a hospital keeps patient details, a bank stores customer transactions, and a business records its sales and stock. All of them need their information stored, updated, searched and managed so the organisation runs smoothly.

Before computers, all of this was done by hand. Data was written on paper and kept in files, registers and folders, usually arranged by date, name or category. It worked, but it was slow: manual record-keeping took a long time, was hard to update, and searching through it was slower still.

A database system solves these problems by storing the data electronically in a structured way, so it can be found, changed and shared quickly. This chapter covers what a database is, why it matters, and how to create and query one using SQL.

blocks.title: The question to keep in mind
blocks.text: Nearly every topic in this chapter answers the same question: what goes wrong when the same data is stored in more than one place? Duplicated data wastes space, and when one copy is updated and another is not, the data stops agreeing with itself. Most of the DBMS features you will learn exist to prevent exactly that.

Open with the manual-versus-electronic contrast: ask what happens when a student changes address and the school holds three paper files. Someone will say "you update all three" — then ask what happens when one is missed. That is data inconsistency, and it motivates the whole chapter.

sections.title: Definition, Importance and Application of Database

blocks.text: An organised collection of data that can be easily accessed, managed and updated — a collection of interrelated data about a place, person or thing, arranged so that an application program such as a DBMS can reach it.

A student database stores roll numbers, names, classes and marks. A bank database stores customer accounts, transactions and balances. The common idea is that the data is related and organised, not just heaped together.
Importance of a database

items: Organised data storage — data is kept in a structured, predictable way.
Easy access — users find and retrieve what they need quickly.
Data sharing — several users can work with the same data at the same time.
Data security — access can be controlled and the data protected.
Reduced redundancy — each fact is stored once instead of being copied into many files.
Data integrity — rules keep the data accurate and consistent.
Backup and recovery — data can be restored after a failure.

blocks.text: Applications of databases

items: Education — student records, examination results and course details.
Hospitals — patient information, doctor schedules and medical history.
E-commerce — product details, customer data and order history.
Government — citizen records and tax data.
Airlines and railways — ticket booking and schedule management.
Telecommunication — call details, billing information and customer accounts.

blocks.text: Data
A collection of raw, unprocessed facts and figures — numbers, text and symbols that have not yet been given meaning.
Information
Data that has been processed, organised and given meaning, so that it is useful for making decisions.

The distinction is best seen with an example. Marks in different subjects — English 4.0, Nepali 2.4, Science 2.0 — are data. The statement "the student passed with a 2.9 GPA" is information. Likewise, temperature readings of 20°C, 22°C and 25°C are data; "today will be warm and sunny" is information.

blocks.caption: Data compared with information

blocks.text: Characteristics of good information
Information is only "good" if it is useful: it must be accurate, complete, relevant to the decision at hand, up to date, and presented in a form the reader can act on.
Database
A collection of related information about a subject, organised in a useful manner so that it provides a base for retrieving information, drawing conclusions and making decisions.
Database system
A database system is the data plus the set of application programs that access, update and manage it. The major uses of database application software are:

items: Data storage and organisation — holding large amounts of data in tables, records and fields, which reduces redundancy.
Data retrieval — searching quickly for specific information using queries.
Data manipulation — inserting, updating and deleting records to keep them accurate.
Reporting — producing documents and summaries from the stored data.

blocks.text: DBMS
Software that lets users create files, update records and retrieve data as requested. It acts as the interface between the application program and the data in the database.
Examples include Microsoft Access, Oracle, MySQL, SQL Server, dBase and FoxPro.

head: Feature
Database
DBMS
rows: The organised collection of data itself
The software that manages the database
Creates, maintains and controls access to the information
A student database with names and marks

blocks.text: The data storage hierarchy
Data is built up in levels, each made from the one below:

items: A bit is the smallest unit of memory — either 0 or 1.
A character is a collection of 8 bits, representing a letter, a number or a symbol.
A field (data item or data element) holds one attribute of an entity; it is often called an attribute.
A record is a collection of related fields forming one complete unit of information.
A file is a collection of related records.
A database is a collection of integrated files.

blocks.title: Learn the hierarchy in one line
blocks.text: Bits → characters → fields → records → files → database. Each level is a collection of the one before it.
The file processing system and its problems

In a file processing system, each application kept its own independent data files, and separate programs updated those files. This is the flat file approach, and it works for one user on a small system. It breaks down as soon as the system grows, because changing a field means changing it in every file that holds a copy.

head: Problem
What it means
Example
rows: The same data is stored in several files, wasting space
A student's address held in both the registration file and the exam file
Copies of the same data hold different values
The address is updated in one file but not the other
Getting an answer requires a new program
Data is scattered across files in different formats
Access control is difficult to enforce
Anyone with the file can read everything
A failure can lose the data for good
A crash destroys the only copy
blocks.caption: Problems with the file processing system

blocks.text: These problems are why the relational database management system (RDBMS) was developed. In an RDBMS the database is made of a set of tables, and the data in one table is linked to other tables through a common field.
Advantages of a DBMS

items: Data can be shared — the same data is available to several users at once, with concurrent access supported.
Data redundancy control — information is stored once in a central database, which keeps it consistent and saves space.
Data integrity — constraints such as primary key, foreign key and check keep the data accurate and prevent invalid entries.
Data security — access can be restricted and controlled.
Backup and recovery — data can be restored after a failure or crash.
Efficient access — indexing and query processing retrieve data quickly.

blocks.text: Students routinely write "reduces redundancy" without explaining how. Push them to the mechanism: store a fact once in one table, and let other tables refer to it by key. That single idea explains both redundancy control and integrity.

blocks.caption: Relationship between field, record and file

blocks.text: A definition of the kind of value a column can hold — number, text, date and so on — and of how much space it uses.
Choosing the right data type matters: it decides what may be stored, how much room the data takes, and which operations make sense on it.
The main data types

Data type
Description
Example

blocks.caption: Common database data types

blocks.title: CHAR versus VARCHAR
blocks.text: CHAR(n) always uses the full n characters, padding short values with spaces, so it suits fixed-length data such as a yes/no flag. VARCHAR(n) stores only what you give it, up to n, so it suits names and addresses where length varies.
Storing a mark as DECIMAL(5,2) allows up to five digits with two after the decimal point, so 100.00 fits but 1000.00 does not.
A relational database stores everything in tables. Understanding what a table is made of is the foundation for the rest of the chapter.
Table
A database object that stores data in rows (records) and columns (fields).
Rows (records)
Each row is one complete record. It holds all the information about one item or person — for example, the row (1, Roshani, 18, Pokhara).
Columns (fields)
Each column is one attribute of the data, and it defines what type of value is stored. For example, Roll_No, Name, Age and Address.

blocks.title: Rows, columns and the vocabulary
blocks.text: Examiners mix these words deliberately. A row is also a record or a tuple; a column is also a field or an attribute. A table is also called a relation. Learn all four pairs — questions often ask for "another name for a row".
A field, or a set of fields, used to identify a record uniquely in a table and to create relationships between tables.
Keys let you find a particular record quickly and keep the connections between tables intact.
Primary key
The primary key uniquely identifies each record in its table. It cannot be repeated and it cannot be left empty. Example: Student_ID in the Students table.
Foreign key
A foreign key links two tables together. It is a field in one table that refers to the primary key in another table.
Student_ID in a Marks table can be a foreign key referring to Roll_No in the Students table. This is what stops a mark being recorded for a student who does not exist.
Candidate key
All the fields that could uniquely identify a record are candidate keys. One of them is chosen as the primary key.
In a Student table both Roll_No and Email might identify a student uniquely, so both are candidate keys.
Alternate key
The candidate keys that were not chosen as the primary key are the alternate keys.
If Roll_No is chosen as the primary key, then Email becomes an alternate key.
Composite key
A key made from more than one field, used when no single field identifies a record uniquely.

blocks.title: Primary key versus foreign key
blocks.text: A primary key identifies a record within its own table. A foreign key points across to the primary key of another table. The primary key is the thing being pointed at; the foreign key does the pointing.

The relationship diagram at the top of the chapter (one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-one, many-to-many) belongs with keys, not before them: a relationship is only implementable once one side has a primary key and the other holds it as a foreign key.
Table, query and report
Three ideas cover most of what people do with a database.
Table

items: Stores data in rows and columns.
Each table has a primary key, for example Student_ID.
Tables hold the raw data, which is inserted, updated and deleted there.

short.q: Define database and DBMS.
short.a:
A database is an organised collection of related data that can be easily accessed, managed and updated. It is more than a pile of facts: the data is interrelated and arranged so that programs can find and use it.

A DBMS (Database Management System) is the software that creates and manages that database. It lets users create files, update records and retrieve data as requested, and it acts as the interface between the application program and the data.

In short: the database is the data, the DBMS is the software that manages it. Examples of a DBMS are MySQL, Oracle and MS Access.

short.q: Write any two differences between a file processing system and a DBMS.
short.a:
BasisFile processing systemDBMS
Data storageEach application keeps its own separate files, so the same data is copied repeatedlyData is stored once centrally and shared
Redundancy and consistencyHigh redundancy, which leads to inconsistent copiesRedundancy is controlled, so data stays consistent
Accessing dataGetting a new answer usually means writing a new programQueries in SQL retrieve data quickly without new programs
Security and recoveryDifficult to enforce access control; a crash can lose dataAccess is controlled, and backup and recovery are provided

short.q: Define relationship in a database.
short.a:
A relationship is the association between two entities in a database — it describes how the rows of one table connect to the rows of another.

Examples: a student takes a class, a teacher teaches a course, and a department employs a teacher.

The four types are one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-one and many-to-many. In practice a relationship is implemented by placing the primary key of one table into the other table as a foreign key.

short.q: Define primary key and foreign key with examples.
short.a:
A primary key is a field that uniquely identifies each record in its own table. It cannot be duplicated and cannot be left empty. Example: Student_ID in a Students table, where every student has a different ID.

A foreign key is a field in one table that refers to the primary key of another table, linking the two. Example: Student_ID in a Marks table is a foreign key referring to Student_ID in Students.

The foreign key is what stops a mark being recorded for a student who does not exist — the database rejects any value that is not present in the parent table.

short.q: What is SQL?
short.a:
SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for accessing and manipulating a relational database. It lets users retrieve data without needing to know how the records are physically stored or how the DBMS carries out the request.

SQL covers four kinds of work: querying data (SELECT), manipulating data (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), defining data (CREATE, ALTER, DROP) and controlling access (GRANT, REVOKE).

short.q: Write any two advantages of a DBMS.
short.a:
Controls data redundancy. Data is stored once in a central database and shared, instead of being copied into separate files. That saves space and keeps copies from disagreeing.

Maintains data integrity. Constraints such as primary keys, foreign keys and CHECK rules keep the data accurate and prevent invalid values from being entered.

Other valid answers include data sharing with concurrent access, data security, backup and recovery, and faster access through indexing and query processing.

short.q: Define any two applications of databases in real life.
short.a:
Education. Schools and colleges use databases to manage student records, examination results and course details.

Hospitals. Patient information, doctor schedules and medical history are held in a database so staff can find them immediately.

Other common applications: e-commerce (products, customers, orders), government (citizen and tax records), airlines and railways (bookings and schedules), and telecommunications (call details and billing).

short.q: Define the terms field and record.
short.a:
A field is the smallest unit of data in a database. It represents a single attribute and appears as one column. Each value in that column is a field value — for example Student_ID, Name, Age or Class.

A record is a collection of related fields, forming one complete row and holding all the information about a single entity. One student's ID, name, age and class together make one record.

short.q: Define the terms entity and attribute.
short.a:
An entity is a real-world object or thing about which data is stored — something that exists and can be recorded, such as a student, a teacher, a course or a product. An entity usually becomes a table.

An attribute is a property or characteristic of that entity, such as a student's name, age or address. Attributes become the fields (columns) of the table.

long.q: What is a database key? Explain how keys help maintain data accuracy and relationships among tables.
long.a:
A key is a field, or a set of fields, used to identify a record uniquely in a table and to build relationships between tables.

The main types:

  • Primary key — uniquely identifies each record in its own table; it cannot repeat and cannot be empty.
  • Foreign key — a field in one table that refers to the primary key of another, linking the two.
  • Candidate key — any field that could serve as the primary key.
  • Alternate key — a candidate key not chosen as the primary key.
  • Composite key — two or more fields used together to identify a record.

How keys keep data accurate. Because a primary key must be unique and present, two records can never share an identity and no record can exist without one. That alone prevents duplicates and half-finished entries. Foreign keys extend the same guarantee across tables: the database refuses any value that does not exist in the parent table, so an order cannot refer to a customer who is not on file. Together these rules are what data integrity means in practice.

How keys build relationships. A relationship is implemented by placing the primary key of one table into another as a foreign key. Putting Customer_ID into the Orders table connects every order to the customer who placed it. That single mechanism implements one-to-many relationships, and with a linking table it implements many-to-many as well.

So a key does two jobs at once: it identifies a row within its own table, and it is the handle by which other tables refer to it.

long.q: Define data redundancy. Explain how a DBMS reduces it.
long.a:
Data redundancy is the unnecessary repetition of data — the same fact stored in more than one place.

It causes two problems. It wastes storage space, and it creates data inconsistency: when one copy is updated and another is not, the copies stop agreeing. A student's address held in both a registration file and an examination file is the textbook example — change it in one place and the other silently goes stale.

How a DBMS reduces redundancy:

  • Centralised storage. Each fact is recorded once in one table, and every application reads it from there instead of keeping its own copy.
  • Normalisation. Data is organised into related tables so that each fact lives in exactly one place — students in one table, courses in another.
  • Relationships through keys. Instead of repeating a student's details in the marks table, that table stores only the Student_ID, which points back to the single copy. The data is shared by reference, not duplicated.
  • Integrity constraints. Primary and foreign keys keep the references correct, so updates are made once and are seen everywhere.

The practical result: update the address once, and every report, query and application sees the new value.

long.q: Define database. Explain any three points on the importance of a database.
long.a:
A database is an organised collection of interrelated data that can be easily accessed, managed and updated. It is arranged so that an application program such as a DBMS can retrieve and use it.

Three reasons databases matter:

1. Organised storage and easy access. Data is held in a structured way — tables, records and fields — so the information needed can be found quickly rather than searched for by hand across piles of paper.

2. Data sharing with reduced redundancy. Several users can work with the same data at the same time, and because each fact is stored once, the copies cannot fall out of step. This is what makes a shared school or bank system possible.

3. Security, integrity and recovery. Access can be restricted to authorised users, rules keep the data accurate and valid, and backups allow the data to be restored after a failure or crash.

Together these turn data from a record of what happened into something an organisation can rely on to make decisions.

long.q: Define DML. Explain any three types of SQL DML commands.
long.a:
DML (Data Manipulation Language) is the part of SQL that works on the data stored in tables — adding, changing, deleting or viewing records — as opposed to DDL, which defines the structure that holds them.

1. INSERT — add new records. Adds one or more rows to a table. You may name the columns, or omit the list if you supply a value for every column in order.

2. SELECT — retrieve data. Fetches data from one or more tables. It can choose particular columns, filter rows with WHERE, sort with ORDER BY, match text patterns with LIKE, and summarise with aggregate functions such as COUNT, SUM and AVG.

3. UPDATE — change existing records. Modifies values in rows that are already there. The WHERE clause decides which rows change; without it, every row in the table is updated, which is why the WHERE clause matters so much.

DELETE is the fourth: it removes rows, again filtered by WHERE. The important contrast for exams is that DELETE removes rows while the table remains, whereas DROP removes the table itself.

practical.q: Create the STUDENT table with the constraints given.
practical.a:
The table needs sid as the primary key, name marked NOT NULL, a check that marks are not negative, and appropriate types for faculty and age.

CREATE TABLE Student (
  sid     INT PRIMARY KEY,
  name    VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
  faculty VARCHAR(30),
  age     INT,
  marks   INT CHECK (marks >= 0)
);

practical.q: Insert five records into the Student table.
practical.a:
Insert five rows in a single statement.

INSERT INTO Student (sid, name, faculty, age, marks) VALUES
  (1, 'Roshan', 'Science',    20, 78),
  (2, 'Sita',   'Management', 19, 65),
  (3, 'Ram',    'Science',    21, 42),
  (4, 'Gita',   'Humanities', 22, 88),
  (5, 'Kiran',  'Computer',   18, 55);

practical.q: Display all records from the Student table.
practical.a:
Select every column of every row.

SELECT * FROM Student;

practical.q: Display only the name and marks of all students.
practical.a:
Name the two columns you want instead of using *.

SELECT name, marks FROM Student;

practical.q: Display students whose age is greater than 20.
practical.a:
Filter with a WHERE clause.

SELECT * FROM Student WHERE age > 20;

practical.q: Display students from the science faculty.
practical.a:
Match the faculty value exactly.

SELECT * FROM Student WHERE faculty = 'Science';

practical.q: Show the details of students who scored more than 60 marks.
practical.a:
Filter on the marks column.

SELECT * FROM Student WHERE marks > 60;

practical.q: Display student details sorted by name.
practical.a:
ORDER BY with ASC for alphabetical order.

SELECT * FROM Student ORDER BY name ASC;

practical.q: Find students whose name starts with the letter R.
practical.a:
Use LIKE with the % wildcard after the letter.

SELECT * FROM Student WHERE name LIKE 'R%';

practical.q: Display students whose age is between 18 and 22.
practical.a:
BETWEEN is inclusive of both ends.

SELECT * FROM Student WHERE age BETWEEN 18 AND 22;

practical.q: Display students ordered by marks in descending order.
practical.a:
ORDER BY with DESC.

SELECT * FROM Student ORDER BY marks DESC;

practical.q: Find the number of students whose marks are above the average.
practical.a:
Compare each row against a subquery that computes the average.

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Student
WHERE marks > (SELECT AVG(marks) FROM Student);

practical.q: Display the names of students who are not from the Computer faculty.
practical.a:
Use NOT with the comparison.

SELECT name FROM Student WHERE faculty <> 'Computer';

practical.q: Increase the marks of all students by 5.
practical.a:
An UPDATE with no WHERE clause changes every row — which is exactly what this question asks for.

UPDATE Student SET marks = marks + 5;

practical.q: Change the name PRR to RRP.
practical.a:
Use WHERE to touch only that one row.

UPDATE Student SET name = 'RRP' WHERE name = 'PRR';

practical.q: Delete students whose marks are less than 40.
practical.a:
A filtered DELETE.

DELETE FROM Student WHERE marks < 40;

practical.q: Create a STUDENT table with RollNo, Name, Class, Section, DOB and Address.
practical.a:
Choose a type for each column: numbers for RollNo and Class, text for the rest, and a DATE for the date of birth. This exercise is named StudentInfo below so that it does not clash with the Student table used in the previous set — the two have different columns, and reusing one name would overwrite it.

CREATE TABLE StudentInfo (
  RollNo  INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Name    VARCHAR(50),
  Class   INT,
  Section VARCHAR(10),
  DOB     DATE,
  Address VARCHAR(100)
);

practical.q: Insert five records into STUDENT and display them.
practical.a:
Insert five rows, then retrieve them.

INSERT INTO StudentInfo VALUES
  (1, 'Anita Shrestha', 10, 'A', '2008-05-14', 'Kathmandu'),
  (2, 'Bibek Thapa',    10, 'B', '2008-01-22', 'Lalitpur'),
  (3, 'Chandra Rai',    10, 'A', '2007-11-03', 'Bhaktapur'),
  (4, 'Dipika Gurung',  10, 'C', '2008-07-09', 'Pokhara'),
  (5, 'Elisha Tamang',  10, 'B', '2007-09-30', 'Dharan');

SELECT * FROM StudentInfo;

practical.q: Display students whose class is 12, and those whose name starts with A.
practical.a:
One filtered query and one pattern-matching query.

SELECT * FROM StudentInfo WHERE Class = 12;

SELECT * FROM StudentInfo WHERE Name LIKE 'A%';

practical.a:
EmpID is the primary key; Salary is numeric and JoinDate is a date.

mcq.teacher_note: The other three are problems a DBMS exists to remove.

blocks.text: Every day we use digital devices — mobile phones, computers, televisions — to watch videos, listen to music, read text and look at pictures. An online class or a learning app may include text notes, images, recorded audio, videos and animations all at once. Websites, advertisements, video games and educational videos combine sound, pictures and moving visuals to make information more interesting, attractive and easier to understand.

That combination has a name. Multimedia is the use of several different kinds of content — text, images, audio, video and animation — together in one presentation or application. This chapter takes it apart: what the components are, what file formats store them, and which software is used to make and edit them.

blocks.title: Why "multi" matters
blocks.text: The power is not in any single element but in the combination. A diagram explains what a paragraph cannot; a short animation explains what a static diagram cannot. Choosing the right medium for each idea is the actual skill.
The integration of text, graphics, audio, video and animation into a single computer-based application, so that information can be presented and interacted with in more than one way at once.
A multimedia system is usually interactive: the user does not only watch, but chooses what to see next, when to pause and what to revisit.
Applications of multimedia
1. Education

Multimedia is used in e-learning platforms, interactive tutorials and digital classrooms. Educational software includes videos, animations and simulations that make learning easier and more interesting, and students can perform virtual experiments or use educational games.
Smart classrooms, online courses.
2. Entertainment
One of the largest applications of multimedia — films, streaming, games and music all combine moving visuals with sound.
3. Business
Presentations, product demonstrations and training material use multimedia to explain products and processes more persuasively than text alone.
4. Advertising and marketing

Multimedia enables eye-catching advertisements that attract customers, combining text, audio, video and animation to deliver a promotional message. It is used in digital marketing, social media campaigns and television commercials.
YouTube ads, animated online product banners.
5. Healthcare
Used for medical training, patient education and surgical simulations. Doctors use 3D imaging and animations to explain medical conditions and procedures.
6. Communication
Multimedia enables modern communication such as video calls, voice messages and social media sharing. It improves clarity and engagement compared with plain text.
Zoom meetings, WhatsApp video calls, YouTube tutorials.
7. Research and engineering
Used to visualise complex data, simulate processes and model prototypes. Engineers use multimedia in CAD (Computer-Aided Design) and virtual simulations for better analysis.
Car design simulations.
Advantages of multimedia

items: Improves learning and understanding — combining text, audio, video and graphics makes complex topics easier to grasp.
More attractive and engaging — interactive content keeps users interested and raises attention and motivation.
Better communication — ideas are explained with visuals and sound, which reduces misunderstanding.
Improves retention — people remember information better when they both see and hear it.

blocks.text: Disadvantages of multimedia

items: Cost — producing good multimedia needs expensive software, hardware and skilled people.
Large file sizes — audio and video take up a lot of storage and bandwidth.
Time — designing and editing quality content takes far longer than writing text.
Compatibility — files may not play correctly on every device or in every player.
Distraction — poorly designed multimedia can distract from the message rather than support it.

blocks.text: Start the chapter with the two discussion questions on the first page: why an online class beats a book alone, and what the shared feature of an advert and an educational video is. Students will arrive at "several media at once" themselves, which is a better definition than one you give them.
Multimedia consists of several components combined together to create an interactive and engaging presentation. The main components are text, graphics, audio, video and animation.
1. Text

Text can be a word, a single line or a paragraph — the original words of a written or printed work. It is the easiest component to create, and any text editor will do. Text in multimedia can vary in type, size, colour and style, and it is what carries the precise detail: names, numbers, definitions and instructions.
2. Graphics

Visual representations of data or ideas — pictures, drawings, charts and illustrations — used to communicate a message and improve the user experience. Graphics carry what words describe poorly: layout, shape, proportion and mood.
3. Audio
Sound stored digitally: speech, music and sound effects. Audio adds explanation, emphasis and atmosphere, and it is the only component that works while the user is looking somewhere else.
4. Video
Moving images recorded digitally, usually with sound. Video shows processes and events as they happen, which no still image can do.
5. Animation

Moving images created from drawings or models rather than recorded from life. Animation shows things that cannot be filmed at all — the inside of a machine, a process speeded up, or something entirely imaginary.

head: Component
What it carries
Best at
rows: Moving images from drawings or models
blocks.caption: The five components of multimedia

blocks.title: Interactivity is the sixth element
blocks.text: The book lists five components, but what makes multimedia multimedia rather than a slideshow is that the user can respond — choose, pause, replay, explore. The user interface and the software behind it are what provide that.
Visual representations of data or ideas — pictures, drawings, charts or illustrations — used to communicate messages and enhance the user experience.
Raster and vector graphics
Images made up of pixels — tiny dots of colour, each with its own specific colour and position. Best for photographs and detailed images.
Images made using mathematical paths — lines, curves and shapes — rather than pixels. They can be resized without losing quality.

head: Basis
Vector graphics
Raster graphics
rows: Images made using mathematical paths (lines, curves, shapes)
Can be resized without loss of quality
Loses quality (becomes blurry or pixelated) when enlarged
blocks.caption: Vector graphics versus raster graphics

blocks.title: The zoom test
blocks.text: The practical way to tell them apart: enlarge the image. A vector logo stays crisp at any size; a raster photograph breaks up into visible squares. This is why a school logo should be vector but the school photograph cannot be.
Graphics file formats
1. JPEG / JPG (Joint Photographic Experts Group)
A raster format designed for photographs. Its file extension is .jpg or .jpeg.

items: High compression rate — JPEG supports strong compression, which greatly reduces file size, so it is easy to share by email or over the internet.
Good image quality — it maintains acceptable quality at typical compression levels.
Fast web loading — small files load quickly on websites.
No transparency — it does not support transparent backgrounds.
Quality degradation — repeated editing and saving reduces quality, because JPEG uses lossy compression each time.

blocks.text: 2. PNG (Portable Network Graphics)
A raster format with lossless compression, designed for the web. Its file extension is .png.

items: Lossless compression — no loss of image quality when compressing.
Transparency — supports transparent backgrounds, making it ideal for logos and web design.
Colour depth — supports up to 48-bit colour and 16-bit greyscale.
No animation — unlike GIF, PNG does not support animation.
Open standard — non-proprietary and free to use.
Interlacing — supports interlacing, so an image can appear gradually as it downloads.

blocks.text: 3. GIF (Graphics Interchange Format)
A bitmap image format supporting simple animations and limited colours, developed by CompuServe in 1987 for sharing images over the internet. Its file extension is .gif.

items: Lossless compression — no loss of quality.
Limited colour support — only 256 colours, from an 8-bit palette.
Animation support — the format that made short looping web animations common.

blocks.text: 4. SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics)

A vector-based image format that describes two-dimensional graphics using XML. Unlike JPG or PNG, SVG images do not lose quality when resized, because they are made of mathematical shapes — lines, curves and points — instead of pixels. Its file extension is .svg.

items: Vector-based — built from mathematical shapes.
Scalable — infinitely resizable with no quality loss.
Text-based — being XML, it can be edited as text and searched.

blocks.text: Uses of SVG: logos and icons, charts and graphs, infographics, and scalable web graphics.
5. PDF (Portable Document Format)
A universal file format developed by Adobe Systems to present documents containing text, images, graphics and links so that they look the same on any device or platform. Its file extension is .pdf.

items: Platform independent — looks the same everywhere.
Preserves formatting — layout, fonts and images stay as intended.
Large file size — files with many images or graphics can become large.
Compatibility issues with older software — some older programs do not support advanced features.
Not ideal for web content editing — less flexible than HTML for online content.

blocks.text: Uses: e-books and manuals, reports and research papers, invoices and forms, certificates.
6. TIFF (Tagged Image File Format)
A high-quality raster format widely used in publishing, scanning and graphic design. Its file extension is .tiff or .tif.

items: Lossless compression — no loss of quality.
Wide colour depth — supports millions of colours and high bit depths.
Flexible compression options — can compress without quality loss.
Preferred in publishing — printing, scanning and graphic design industries.
Large file size — high-quality TIFF images take a lot of storage.
Not ideal for web use — slow to load and not widely supported by browsers.

blocks.text: 7. BMP (Bitmap)
A simple raster format that stores pixel data with little or no compression. Its file extension is .bmp. It gives accurate images but very large files, so it is rarely used on the web.
Give students one photograph saved as JPG, PNG, GIF and BMP and let them compare file sizes and zoom in to 800 per cent. The differences become obvious in a way a table never achieves.
Sound stored digitally — speech, music and sound effects — so that a computer can play, edit and transmit it.
How sound becomes digital

items: Sound travels in waves — vibrations moving through air or another medium.
A microphone or audio recorder converts these sound waves into electrical signals (analog) or digital signals (numbers).
When displayed on a screen, the changing signal looks like a waveform.

Description
rows: Height of the wave — represents loudness. Higher amplitude means louder sound.
Number of waves per second — represents pitch. More waves per second means a higher note.
The distance covered by one complete wave cycle.

These store sound with no compression, giving the best quality at the cost of large files.

blocks.text: MP3 in detail
MP3 is the format students will meet most, so it is worth knowing both sides.
Advantages

items: Small file size — far smaller than WAV, so it saves storage.
Wide compatibility — plays on almost every device and platform.
Portability — small files let you carry hundreds or thousands of songs on a portable device.
Streaming friendly — suitable for streaming over the internet without consuming excessive bandwidth.
Easy editing — can be edited, copied and shared across devices and platforms.

blocks.text: Disadvantages

items: Lossy compression — MP3 removes some audio data, so quality is lower than the original.
Not suitable for professional recording — studios work with uncompressed audio.
Quality loss increases at low bitrates — the more you compress, the worse it sounds.

sections.title: Video: Frame Rate, Resolution and File Formats

blocks.text: A type of digital file that stores moving visual images, often together with audio, subtitles and metadata.

Each video file has two parts that are easy to confuse: the container, such as MP4 or AVI, which is the file itself, and the codec, such as H.264 or HEVC, which compresses and decompresses the video data inside it.

blocks.title: Container versus codec
blocks.text: The container is the box; the codec is how the contents were packed. A file being ".mp4" tells you the box, not which codec is inside — which is why a video sometimes will not play even though the extension looks right.
Frame rate
The number of individual frames, or still images, displayed per second. It is measured in frames per second (fps).
A video is really a sequence of still pictures shown fast enough that the eye sees continuous motion. How many pictures per second decides how smooth that motion looks.

head: Frame rate
Typical use
Effect
rows: Standard, smooth enough for most content
Very smooth; better for rapid movement
blocks.caption: Common frame rates

blocks.text: Why frame rate matters

items: Smoothness — more frames per second means smoother motion.
File size — more frames means more data, so the file is bigger.
System performance — a high frame rate needs more processing power (CPU/GPU); a low frame rate works better on low-end devices.
User experience — a high frame rate improves viewing, especially in games and sports; a low frame rate may cause eye strain or discomfort during fast motion.

blocks.text: Resolution
The number of pixels that make up the width and height of a video image. It determines the clarity and detail of the picture.

Higher resolution gives a sharper, more detailed picture and an enhanced viewing experience — it is ideal for movies, sports and high-quality content. The cost is a larger file and more processing power.
Video file formats

items: MP4 (.mp4) — the most universal format; works on phones, TVs and computers; usually uses H.264 or H.265; best for sharing and streaming.
AVI (.avi) — an older format; larger files and less compression.
MOV (.mov) — developed by Apple; high quality, commonly used in video editing.
MKV (.mkv) — an open container that can hold many audio, video and subtitle tracks.
WMV (.wmv) — Windows Media Video, used mainly on Windows.
WebM (.webm) — an open format designed for the web.

blocks.text: Moving images created from drawings or models, shown in sequence so that they appear to move.
Animation shows what a camera cannot record: the inside of a machine, a process slowed down or speeded up, or something that does not exist at all.
Common animation file formats

items: GIF (.gif) — simple web-based animations.
SWF (.swf) — Adobe Flash animations.
MP4 (.mp4) — animated videos.
MOV (.mov) — high-quality video animations.
AVI (.avi) — a standard animation/video format.

blocks.text: Advantages of animation

items: Better understanding of concepts — animation explains complex ideas easily.
Attractive and engaging — moving visuals grab attention more effectively than still ones.
Shows the invisible — processes too small, too slow, too fast or simply imaginary can be shown.

blocks.text: Disadvantages of animation

items: Time-consuming — creating high-quality animation requires a lot of time for designing, modelling and editing.
High production cost — professional software and skilled animators are expensive.
Requires technical skills — animation needs knowledge of design, software tools and creativity.
Large file size — high-quality animated video, especially HD or 3D, takes a lot of storage.

blocks.text: 2D animation
Flat animation in two dimensions — height and width. It works on a flat plane with no depth.
Common software
Adobe Animate, Toon Boom Harmony, Pencil2D, Synfig Studio.
Examples
Classic cartoons such as Tom and Jerry or Mickey Mouse, educational animations and 2D games.
Advantages

items: Simple to create — easier than 3D because it works in two dimensions.
Lower production cost — usually needs a smaller budget than 3D.
Less hardware requirement — does not need a very powerful computer.

blocks.text: 3D animation
Animation in three dimensions with depth and volume. Objects can be rotated and viewed from any angle.
Features

items: It uses realistic 3D models with depth and volume.
Movements and camera angles can be fully controlled.
Lighting, shadows and textures make visuals more lifelike.

blocks.text: Common software
Autodesk Maya, Blender, Cinema 4D, 3ds Max.
Examples
Pixar films such as Toy Story or Finding Nemo, modern video games, and 3D advertisements and visual effects in films.
Disadvantages

items: High production cost — 3D needs expensive software and skilled professionals.
Time-consuming — modelling, rigging, texturing and rendering take a long time.
Needs powerful hardware — high-performance computers are required for a smooth workflow.
Complex to learn — requires advanced technical knowledge and training.

blocks.text: Show the same short scene as 2D and as 3D — a cartoon and a Pixar clip — and ask which was cheaper to make and why. Students usually guess correctly and can then articulate the cost difference.

Adobe Photoshop is the most popular program for creating and modifying images for the web. It is available on a wide variety of platforms, from Mac to Windows. It is the predominant photo editing and manipulation software on the market, and its uses range from full-featured editing of large groups of photos to creating complex digital paintings and drawings done by hand. It is a critical tool for designers, web developers and photographers.
The Photoshop interface
The menu bar

The Photoshop menu bar consists of File, Edit, Image, Layer, Select, View, Window and Help. It works much like the menu bar in any other application, and it follows the standard keyboard shortcuts you would expect: ALT+F accesses the File menu, and Ctrl+N opens the New dialog from the File menu.
The drawing canvas

The drawing canvas is the area in which you work. It is the workspace around an existing image, within the image window. Layer data may lie outside the canvas, but it will be clipped to the canvas when the image is flattened.
Every drawing canvas has a title bar with window control buttons and a drawing area. The title bar shows the current name of the image along with information about the colour mode and zoom scale.
To open a new canvas, click "File", then "New". The New Canvas dialog appears. Give the canvas a name, set the height and width, and click OK — the new canvas then appears.
The toolbox

The Photoshop toolbox holds around 20 tools that let you paint, select, navigate and edit images. To select a tool, click its icon. The selected tool button stays depressed so you can see which is active.
Palettes

Photoshop palettes share several properties. All palettes are made up of a title bar with close and collapse buttons, a set of tabs, and a list of options for each tab, and all have a fly-out menu of options. You can also customise any palette by dragging tabs between palettes.
Drawing on the canvas

Photoshop uses a carefully constructed metaphor that turns a complex computer-aided task into a fun and easy-to-understand process: a blank canvas, a table full of differently shaped brushes, and paint. To customise a brush you use the "options" palette. The most common change is to the brush size, which you set from the Brushes tab by choosing a larger or smaller brush from the range given. Except for the Pencil tool, brush shapes are always anti-aliased, so you can choose either a hard edge (solid) or a soft edge (blended).
Changing image size
Image size refers to the length and width of a digital image — its pixel dimensions.

blocks.title: Changing image size
items: Open the required image file.
Click Image menu > Image Size… (shortcut: Alt+I, then select Image Size). An Image Size dialog box appears, showing the current pixel dimensions, print size and resolution.
Type the required Width and Height in the Pixel Dimensions section. If "Constrain Proportions" is checked, entering the width sets the height proportionally.
Change the Width and Height in the Document Size section if you intend to print the image.

blocks.title: Enlarging a small image cannot add detail
blocks.text: Increasing the size of a low-resolution image produces a low-quality result: the pixels are simply spread out. Always start from the largest, highest-resolution original you have.
Changing the file format

blocks.title: Changing the file format
items: Open the image file whose format you want to change.
Click File menu > Save As… (Ctrl+Shift+S). A Save As dialog box appears.
Type a name in the File Name box if you want a different one.
Select the folder to save in, if you want a different location.
Select the file format you want.
Click Save.

blocks.text: Creating a new image file

blocks.title: Creating a new image file
items: Click File menu > New… (shortcut: Ctrl+N). A New dialog box appears.
Type the required values for width, height and resolution.
Select the Colour Mode and Background Contents.
Click OK. A blank image file appears in the workspace.

blocks.text: Useful tools

The toolbox contains groups of tools for editing and manipulating images. The character in brackets next to a tool is its shortcut key — press C, for example, to activate the Crop tool. Select a tool by clicking its icon; if an icon has a small triangle at its lower right, hold the mouse button down to reveal the hidden tools beneath it.

head: Tool
What it does
rows: Adds text to an image — useful for posters, invitations and other graphic work
Selects a rectangular area, which can then be copied, cut or filled
Selects parts of an image based on colour — touch the desired colour and areas of the same colour are selected
Adjusts the overall size of an image by removing unnecessary outer parts; affects the whole image, not one layer
Copies pixels from one part of an image to another
Moves a layer or a selection
blocks.caption: Some Photoshop tools

blocks.text: To show or hide the toolbox, choose Window > Tools — a check mark in the menu indicates the item is showing. Drag the toolbox by its title bar to move it. Tool tips can be turned on or off from Edit > Preferences > General (in Windows) or Photoshop > Preferences > General (in Mac OS) by selecting or deselecting "Show Tool Tips".
Working with text

blocks.title: Working with text
items: Type the required text using the Type tool.
To move the text, select the text layer, select the Move tool (or press V), then click and drag the text to position it.
To edit the text, double-click the layer icon for that text, or select the Type tool and click the text. The text is highlighted and you can modify the wording, size and colour.

blocks.text: Audio editing software is a computer program used to record, modify, manipulate and enhance audio files. One of the most popular is Audacity.
Free, open-source audio recording and editing software, used for recording sound, editing audio files and applying audio effects.
It is widely used by students, teachers, podcasters, musicians and audio editors because it is free and runs on Windows, macOS and Linux.
Features of Audacity

items: Recording — record from a microphone or from the computer’s own audio.
Editing — cut, copy, paste, split and trim audio clips.
Effects — fade in and out, noise reduction, speed and pitch change, amplification and more.
Multi-track editing — work with several tracks at once, for voice over music for example.
Formats supported — WAV, MP3, AIFF, FLAC and OGG.
Exporting — export in different formats, setting the bitrate, quality and file name; suitable for podcasts, music and presentations.

blocks.text: The Audacity interface

items: Menu bar — provides access to all commands.
Toolbar — contains the record, play, pause and stop tools.
Track control panel — controls mute, solo, volume and pan for each track.
Waveform display — shows the audio visually, so you can see where speech and silence are.

blocks.text: Installing Audacity

blocks.title: Installing Audacity
items: Open your web browser and go to the official Audacity website.
Click the Download Audacity button.
Find the downloaded executable file in your Downloads folder and run it.
Confirm that you allow the program to make changes to your system by clicking Yes.
Follow the remaining on-screen prompts to finish the installation.

blocks.text: CapCut is one of the most popular video editing programs. It is used to create, edit and enhance video files by arranging clips and adding effects, transitions, audio and text.
A free, user-friendly video editing application developed by ByteDance, used to create and edit videos easily on mobile phones and computers.
It is popular among students, content creators and social media users because it provides professional features with simple tools.
Features of CapCut

items: Easy video editing — cut, trim, split and merge clips using a timeline.
Text and titles — add text, captions, subtitles and animated titles.
Transitions — smooth transitions such as fade, slide, zoom and blur between clips.
Effects and filters — video effects, filters and visual enhancements.
Audio editing — add background music, sound effects and voice-over, and adjust audio levels.
Templates — ready-made templates for quick video creation.
Export options — export in HD and 4K at different frame rates.

blocks.text: Uses and advantages

items: Creating social media videos (YouTube, TikTok, Instagram).
Making educational and presentation videos.
Editing short films and vlogs.
Creating reels and shorts.
Free to use.
Simple, beginner-friendly interface.
Works on both mobile and PC.
No watermark on exported videos.
Supports high-quality export.

blocks.text: Installing CapCut
Getting CapCut Desktop is quick and works on both Windows and macOS.

blocks.title: Installing CapCut
items: Open your web browser and visit the official CapCut website.
Locate the Download button on the homepage and click it.
Choose your operating system (Windows or Mac) and click the appropriate version to download.
Open your Downloads folder and find the installer file.
Double-click the installer to launch the setup.
Follow the on-screen prompts, select an installation location if asked, and accept the terms and conditions.
Wait for the installation to finish, then open CapCut from your applications.

blocks.text: Editing a video in CapCut
Opening and importing

blocks.title: Opening and importing a video
items: Open CapCut. The home screen shows New Project, Recent Projects and Templates.
Click New Project to begin.
Browse your device storage and choose the video file you want.
Click Add (mobile) or Import (PC) to load the video.
The video appears in the media library and is placed on the timeline.
Play it in the preview window to confirm the import worked.

blocks.text: The timeline

blocks.title: Working with the timeline
items: CapCut creates a timeline automatically at the bottom of the screen once a clip is added.
Drag the timeline left or right to move through the video.
Pinch (mobile) or use the zoom controls (PC) to zoom in and out.
Tap + or Add to insert more video, images or audio.
Use the timeline to cut, trim, split, and add effects, text, transitions and audio.

blocks.text: Cutting and trimming

blocks.title: Cutting and trimming
items: Tap or click the clip on the timeline to select it.
Drag the playhead — the white line — to the point where you want to cut.
Tap Split (the scissors icon) to cut the clip into two parts.
Select the unwanted portion and tap Delete.
Play the video to check the cut, then continue editing or export.

blocks.text: Transitions

blocks.title: Adding transitions
items: Add two or more clips to the timeline — transitions work between clips.
Arrange the clips next to each other.
Tap the small white box, or transition icon, between two clips.
Select a transition type: Fade, Slide, Zoom, Blur or 3D.
Set the duration by dragging the slider or entering a time, then tap Apply.
Play the video to check the effect.

blocks.text: Effects and text

blocks.title: Adding effects and text
items: Select the clip, then tap Effects from the bottom menu and choose Video Effects.

short.q: Define multimedia.
short.a:
Multimedia is the integration of several kinds of content — text, graphics, audio, video and animation — into a single computer-based application, so that information can be presented in more than one way at once.

The key word is integration. A document with a picture in it is not multimedia; an application in which the user watches a clip, reads the explanation, hears the narration and clicks to explore further is.

short.q: List the components of multimedia.
short.a:
The five main components are:

  1. Text — words, lines and paragraphs.
  2. Graphics — pictures, drawings, charts and illustrations.
  3. Audio — digitally stored sound: speech, music and effects.
  4. Video — moving images recorded digitally.
  5. Animation — moving images created from drawings or models.

Interactivity — provided by the user interface and the software — is what turns these components into multimedia rather than a slideshow.

short.q: What is an image file format? Give examples.
short.a:
An image file format is a standard way of storing a picture in a file: it defines how the pixel or shape data is arranged and compressed, and it is identified by the file extension.

Examples: JPEG (.jpg) for photographs, PNG (.png) for web graphics with transparency, GIF (.gif) for simple animation, SVG (.svg) for scalable vector graphics, BMP (.bmp) uncompressed, and TIFF (.tiff) for printing.

short.q: Define audio and video in multimedia.
short.a:
Audio is sound stored digitally — speech, music and sound effects — so that a computer can store, play and edit it. It is the component that works while the user is looking elsewhere.

Video is a sequence of moving images recorded digitally, usually with sound. It shows events and processes as they actually happen, which a still image cannot.

short.q: What do you understand by resolution in multimedia?
short.a:
Resolution is the number of pixels that make up the width and height of an image or video frame — for example 1920 × 1080. It determines the clarity and detail of the picture.

More pixels means a sharper image, but also a larger file and more processing power. Resolution is fixed at the time of recording: enlarging a low-resolution image cannot add detail that was never captured.

short.q: What is lossy and lossless compression?
short.a:
Lossy compression reduces file size by permanently discarding some data that is judged least noticeable. It gives much smaller files but the original cannot be fully recovered, and quality degrades further each time the file is re-saved. JPEG, MP3 and AAC are lossy.

Lossless compression reduces file size by storing the same data more efficiently, without discarding anything. The original can be restored exactly. PNG, FLAC and ALAC are lossless.

short.q: Give two examples of multimedia applications in education.
short.a:

E-learning platforms and virtual experiments — students perform simulated experiments and use educational games to practise concepts that would be impractical, expensive or dangerous to do for real.

short.q: What is an image file format? Give two examples.
short.a:
It is the standard by which a picture is stored in a file, defining how the image data is arranged and compressed and what its extension is.

Two examples: JPEG (.jpg), a lossy raster format used for photographs, and SVG (.svg), a vector format that can be scaled without losing quality.

short.q: Name two applications of multimedia in education.
short.a:
Interactive tutorials — software that combines text, narration, diagrams and animation, letting a student work at their own pace.

Digital classrooms and online courses — recorded or live lessons with slides, video and screen demonstration, which make the material available beyond the classroom.

short.q: Write any two importance of multimedia in entertainment.
short.a:
Engagement — combining moving visuals with sound holds attention in a way that text or a still image cannot, which is why films, games and streaming dominate leisure time.

Realism and immersion — 3D animation, effects and surround sound create experiences that feel lifelike, from animated films to modern video games.

short.q: Mention any two advantages of multimedia technology.
short.a:
Improves learning and understanding — combining text, audio, video and graphics makes complex topics easier to grasp.

Better communication and retention — ideas explained with visuals and sound are misunderstood less often and remembered better, because people remember information they have both seen and heard.

long.q: What is 2D animation? Define any three components of multimedia with suitable examples.
long.a:
2D animation is flat animation in two dimensions — height and width. It works on a flat plane with no depth, and it is created by showing a sequence of drawings or digital frames in quick succession. Classic cartoons such as Tom and Jerry, educational animations and 2D games are examples. It is cheaper and quicker to produce than 3D, and needs less powerful hardware.

Three components of multimedia:

Text — the original words of a written work, which can be a word, a line or a paragraph. It carries precise detail: names, numbers, definitions. Example: the labels and captions on a diagram, or the instructions on a screen.

Graphics — visual representations such as pictures, drawings, charts and illustrations. Example: a pie chart of household expenses, or a school logo saved as an SVG.

Audio — sound stored digitally: speech, music and sound effects. Example: the narration over a video lesson, or background music in a presentation.

long.q: What is 3D? Explain different types of multimedia.
long.a:
3D means three-dimensional: an object described with height, width and depth, so that it has volume and can be viewed or rotated from any angle. In 3D animation, realistic models are built, then movements and camera angles are fully controlled, and lighting, shadows and textures make the result look lifelike. Pixar films such as Toy Story, modern video games and 3D advertisements are examples. The cost is high: expensive software, powerful hardware, and a great deal of time for modelling, rigging, texturing and rendering.

Types of multimedia. Multimedia can be grouped by how the user experiences it:

Linear multimedia — content that plays in a fixed sequence with no user control over the order, such as a film or a straightforward slideshow.

Non-linear (interactive) multimedia — the user chooses the path: an educational course, a game, a website or a museum kiosk. This is what the word usually implies in practice, because the interface and software let the user respond.

It can also be classified by what the content is for: educational, entertainment, business, advertising, healthcare, communication, and research and engineering — the seven applications listed in this chapter.

long.q: What is graphics? Explain any three graphics file formats.
long.a:
Graphics are visual representations of data or ideas — pictures, drawings, charts or illustrations — used to communicate a message and improve the user experience. They carry what words describe poorly: layout, shape, proportion and mood.

JPEG (.jpg) — a raster format designed for photographs. It offers a very high compression rate, so files are small and load quickly on the web, but it is lossy: quality degrades each time the file is edited and re-saved. It does not support transparency.

PNG (.png) — a raster format with lossless compression, so no quality is lost. It supports transparent backgrounds, which makes it ideal for logos and web graphics, and it supports up to 48-bit colour. Unlike GIF it has no animation.

SVG (.svg) — a vector format that describes graphics in XML as mathematical lines, curves and shapes. Because there are no pixels, an SVG can be scaled to any size with no loss of quality, and it can be edited as text. It is used for logos, icons, charts and infographics.

long.q: What is animation? Explain audio and video file formats with examples.
long.a:
Animation is the technique of creating moving images from drawings or models, shown in sequence so that they appear to move. It shows what a camera cannot record: the inside of a machine, a process speeded up, or something entirely imaginary. Common file formats are GIF for simple web animations, SWF for Adobe Flash, and MP4, MOV and AVI for animated video.

Audio formats. Uncompressed formats store the sound exactly, at the cost of large files: WAV (.wav), developed by Microsoft and IBM and used in professional recording, and AIFF (.aiff), Apple’s equivalent for Mac systems.

Compressed formats are either lossy or lossless. Lossy examples: MP3 (.mp3), the most popular, balancing quality and size; AAC (.aac), better quality than MP3 at the same size and used by iTunes and YouTube; WMA (.wma), Microsoft’s format for streaming; and OGG (.ogg), an open-source format. Lossless examples: FLAC (.flac) and ALAC (.m4a), which keep every bit of the original while still saving space.

Video formats. MP4 (.mp4) is the most universal, working on phones, TVs and computers, usually with the H.264 or H.265 codec — best for sharing and streaming. AVI (.avi) is older, with larger files and less compression. MOV (.mov), from Apple, is high quality and common in editing. MKV (.mkv) and WebM (.webm) are open containers, and WMV (.wmv) is Windows-oriented.

long.q: What is a vector image? Explain the role of multimedia in education, business, and entertainment.
long.a:
A vector image is one built from mathematical paths — lines, curves and shapes — rather than from pixels. Because the computer stores the instructions for drawing the shapes, not the dots, a vector image is resolution independent: it can be enlarged to any size and stay perfectly sharp. Vector files are usually smaller than raster ones, and SVG is the common vector format for the web.

Education. Multimedia appears in e-learning platforms, interactive tutorials and digital classrooms. Video, animation and simulation make abstract ideas concrete, and virtual experiments let students practise safely and cheaply what would be impractical in a real laboratory. Students retain more when they both see and hear the material.

Business. Multimedia is used for presentations, product demonstrations and staff training. A short animation can explain a process faster than a manual, and a well-made presentation persuades more effectively than a document — which is why PowerPoint is a standard business tool.

Entertainment. This is the largest application of multimedia. Films, streaming, video games and music all combine moving visuals with sound. 3D animation and effects create immersive worlds — from Pixar films to modern games — that would be impossible with any single medium.

long.q: What is a raster image? Explain the concepts of resolution, frame rate, and colour depth in multimedia.
long.a:
A raster image (bitmap) is made of pixels — tiny dots of colour, each with a specific colour and position. Raster images are resolution dependent: they hold a fixed number of dots, so enlarging one makes it blurry or pixelated. JPEG, PNG, GIF and BMP are all raster formats, and photographs are inherently raster.

Resolution is the number of pixels across the width and height of an image or video frame — 1920 × 1080, for example. It sets how much detail the picture holds. More pixels means a sharper image but a larger file, and detail cannot be added later by enlarging a low-resolution original.

Frame rate is how many still images are displayed each second, measured in frames per second (fps). Around 24 fps is the cinema standard; 25–30 fps is normal for television and online video; 50–60 fps suits sport and games. Higher rates look smoother but need more processing power and produce larger files.

Colour depth (bit depth) is how many bits are used to describe the colour of a single pixel, and therefore how many colours the image can show. 8-bit gives 256 colours — which is all a GIF supports — while 24-bit gives roughly 16.7 million, and formats such as PNG go to 48-bit. Greater depth means smoother colour, at the cost of a larger file.

long.q: What is interactive multimedia? Explain the importance of compression in multimedia.
long.a:
Interactive multimedia is multimedia in which the user controls what happens: choosing what to view next, when to pause, what to replay and which path to follow. A film is linear — it plays the same way regardless. An educational course, a game, a website or a museum kiosk responds to the user, and that two-way exchange is what makes it interactive.

Why compression matters. Raw multimedia is enormous. One minute of uncompressed CD-quality stereo audio is about 10 MB, and uncompressed HD video is larger by orders of magnitude. Without compression, storing or streaming it would be impractical on ordinary devices and connections.

Compression therefore makes multimedia usable at all: files are small enough to store in quantity, fast enough to load on a web page, and light enough to stream over a mobile connection. The trade-off is quality. Lossy compression (JPEG, MP3, H.264) discards detail permanently to achieve much smaller files, which is fine for photographs and streamed video. Lossless compression (PNG, FLAC) keeps everything and is used where the original must be preserved exactly. Choosing between them — accepting a little quality loss for a big saving in size — is one of the central practical judgements in multimedia work.

long.q: What is multimedia technology? Explain how text, images, audio, video, and animation are integrated into multimedia systems.
long.a:
Multimedia technology is the combination of hardware and software that captures, stores, processes and presents more than one kind of media at once — and crucially, lets the user interact with the result. It includes input devices such as microphones and cameras, storage, processing hardware, and authoring and playback software.

How the components are integrated. Each element is created in its own tool — text in an editor, images in Photoshop, audio in Audacity, video and animation in an editor such as CapCut. They are then brought together in an authoring application, where they are placed on a common timeline. The timeline is what makes integration possible: it ties each element to a point in time, so that a caption appears exactly when the narration mentions it and a sound effect lands on the right frame.

Text supplies precise detail — labels, captions, subtitles, instructions. Images supply layout and structure that words convey poorly. Audio supplies narration, music and effects, and works while the user looks elsewhere. Video shows real events and processes. Animation shows what cannot be filmed at all.

A user interface — buttons, menus, links and playback controls — sits over the top and lets the user choose, pause and explore. That interface, driven by the software, is what turns five separate media into one multimedia system rather than five files in a folder.

detailed.title: Multimedia
detailed.overview: Multimedia is the integration of text, graphics, audio, video and animation into a single application. This chapter explains what each component is for, which file formats store them and why, and how the standard tools — Photoshop for images, Audacity for audio and CapCut for video — are used to produce and edit multimedia content.
