Define and call functions, and distinguish parameters from arguments.
Explain return values and the scope of local and global variables.
Pass arguments positionally, by keyword, with defaults and with *args.
Import and use standard libraries, and install external ones with pip.
Draw shapes with Turtle using movement, colour and fill commands.
Classify errors and handle exceptions with try, except, else and finally.
Read and write files using the correct mode, and handle CSV data with pandas.
Create line, bar and pie charts with matplotlib and choose the right chart.

blocks.text: Computers calculate expenses, store names, display messages and repeat tasks such as printing a list of numbers. But they do none of this on their own. A computer works only when we give it clear, correct instructions that tell it what to do, step by step — and those instructions must be written in a form the machine can understand.

That is what a programming language is for. Different languages suit different kinds of work. This chapter uses Python, which is a good first language because its syntax reads close to English and because the same language is used in data science, web development, automation and artificial intelligence.

A good programming language should be easy to read and understand. Programs are read far more often than they are written — by the person who wrote them, weeks later, and by other people entirely — so readability is not decoration, it is the main thing.

blocks.title: How this chapter is laid out
blocks.text: It builds in layers: first the basics you need to write any program, then functions to reuse code, then libraries that give you code other people have already written, then graphics, error handling, files and finally charts. Each layer uses the ones before it.

sections.title: Revision of the Basics of Python

blocks.text: What kind of language is Python?

items: It has simple, readable syntax — punctuation and boilerplate are kept to a minimum, and block structure comes from indentation rather than brackets.
It is an interpreted language, so there is no separate compilation step before running a program.
It is dynamically typed, so you do not declare the type of a variable — Python works it out from the value.
It supports both object-oriented and procedural styles.

blocks.text: The working environment
Python programs are written and run using tools called Integrated Development Environments, or IDEs. The common ones are:

items: IDLE — the default editor installed with Python; enough to write, save and run programs.
PyCharm — a powerful IDE for larger projects.
Jupyter Notebook — browser-based, excellent for data science and experimenting interactively.
Google Colab — an online platform from Google that runs Python in the browser with nothing to install.

blocks.text: Python source files always end in .py, for example hello.py. You can run a program from the terminal with python hello.py, or from inside an IDE.
How a Python program runs

When you run a program, the Python interpreter reads the code line by line. It first breaks the code into small pieces called tokens and checks that the syntax is correct. If there are no syntax errors, the code is converted into an intermediate form called bytecode.

That bytecode is then executed by the Python Virtual Machine (PVM), which performs the actual operations — calculations, input and output. Control-flow statements decide the order things happen in, and functions organise the program into reusable blocks.
Identifiers
The name given to a variable, function, class or other object so that the program can refer to it.
Rules for identifiers

items: An identifier must start with a letter (a–z, A–Z) or an underscore (_).
It cannot start with a number.
It may contain only letters, numbers and underscores.
Spaces are not allowed.
Special symbols such as @, #, $ and % are not allowed.
Identifiers are case-sensitive — name and Name are two different things.
Reserved words (keywords) such as if, else, for and while cannot be used as identifiers.

blocks.title: The two mistakes beginners actually make
blocks.text: Using a keyword as a name, and expecting Name and name to be the same variable. Both produce errors that look baffling until you know the rule.
Data types

is_student = True
marks   = [62, 75, 80]
student = ("Sita", 15)
info    = {"name": "Sita", "class": 10}
print(type(is_student), type(marks), type(student), type(info))

blocks.title: list versus tuple
blocks.text: Both hold several items in order, but a list can be changed after creation and a tuple cannot. Use a list for data that will grow or change; use a tuple for a fixed group such as a name and an age that belong together.
Operators
Two of these cause endless confusion: / always gives a float (10 / 2 is 5.0), while // is floor division and gives a whole number (10 // 3 is 3).

x = 10
y = 3
print(x + y)     # 13
print(x / y)     # 3.3333333333333335
print(x // y)    # 3   floor division
print(x % y)     # 1   remainder
print(x ** 3)    # 1000
print(x > y)     # True
Input and output
print() displays output and input() reads it from the user. Note that input() always returns a string, so it must be converted with int() or float() before doing arithmetic with it.

name = input("Enter your name: ")
age  = int(input("Enter your age: "))     # convert, or age is text
print("Hello", name + "!", "You are", age, "years old.")

blocks.title: Why the conversion matters
blocks.text: input() returns text. If you write age = input("Age: ") and then age + 1, Python raises a TypeError, because you cannot add a number to text. This is the single most common beginner error in Python.
Conditional statements
Conditional statements let a program choose what to do.
The elif branches are tested in order, and the first one that is true wins. Because 68 is not ≥ 80 but is ≥ 60, this prints "First Division".

blocks.title: Indentation is not optional
blocks.text: Python uses indentation to define blocks — there are no braces. Every line in a block must be indented by the same amount, and four spaces is the convention. Getting this wrong is a syntax error, not a style issue.
Loops
The for loop
Use a for loop when you know how many times to repeat.

for i in range(1, 6):
    print(i)
range(1, 6) produces 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 — the stop value is not included. That off-by-one is worth pointing out to students the first time they meet it.
The while loop
Use a while loop when you do not know in advance how many times it will run.

i = 1
while i <= 5:
    print(i)
    i += 1
If you forget the i += 1, the condition never becomes false and the loop runs forever.
Lists and looping
Comments

items: A single-line comment starts with #.
A multi-line comment can be written using triple quotes (''' ... ''' or """ ... """).

blocks.text:
# This is a single-line comment
x = 10   # a comment can also follow code

"""
This is a multi-line comment,
used to explain a larger section.
"""
print(x)

Most of this section is revision, so do not lecture through it. Give a five-minute diagnostic: ask for the value of 10 // 3, ask what type input() returns, and ask why the last item of range(1,6) is 5. The answers tell you what to re-teach.

blocks.caption: How Does Python a Program Work?

blocks.text: These programs put the basics together. Each one can be copied and run as it stands.
Program 1 — Average of three numbers

num1 = float(input("Enter first number: "))
num2 = float(input("Enter second number: "))
num3 = float(input("Enter third number: "))
average = (num1 + num2 + num3) / 3
print("The average is:", average)
Program 2 — Greeting with name and age

name = input("Name: ")
age = int(input("Age: "))
print(f"Hello, {name}! You are {age} years old.")
An f-string — the f before the quote — lets you put variables straight into the text inside curly braces. It is the clearest way to build a message.
Program 3 — Swapping two numbers

a = int(input("Enter first number: "))
b = int(input("Enter second number: "))

print("Before swapping: a =", a, " b =", b)
a, b = b, a          # Python swaps in one statement
print("After swapping:  a =", a, " b =", b)
Python assigns the right-hand side as a tuple and unpacks it, which is why no temporary variable is needed.
Program 4 — Biggest of three numbers
Program 5 — Multiplication table
Program 6 — Sum of numbers from 1 to n

n = int(input("Enter a number: "))
total = 0
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    total = total + i
print("The sum of numbers from 1 to", n, "is", total)
Program 7 — Even or odd, and the squares of a list

# Even or odd
n = int(input("Enter a number: "))
if n % 2 == 0:
    print(n, "is even")
else:
    print(n, "is odd")

# Squares of every number in a list
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
squares = [x ** 2 for x in numbers]
print("Squares:", squares)
The second part uses a list comprehension — a compact way to build one list from another. It is the same as a for loop that appends to a list, written in one line.
Program 8 — A number-guessing game

blocks.title: An infinite loop that is meant to be infinite
blocks.text: while True: never ends on its own — the loop exits only when break runs. That is the right pattern when you cannot know in advance how many attempts something will take, but always check there is a reachable break.

Writing the same code over and over makes a program long, confusing and hard to change. If a calculation appears in five places and you then need to fix it, you have five places to edit — and you will miss one.
Python solves this by letting you group related statements into a reusable block called a function.
A block of well-organised, reusable code that performs a specific task. In Python a function is defined with the def keyword.
Built-in functions
Python already provides many functions, so you do not have to write them:

items: print() — displays output on the screen.
input() — reads input from the user.
len() — returns the length of a string or list.
sum() — calculates the sum of the elements.
type() — tells you the type of a value.

blocks.text: Defining and calling a function

def greet():
    print("Hello!")
    print("Welcome to Python.")

greet()      # calling the function runs the code inside it
greet()      # you can call it as often as you like
Defining a function does not run it. The code inside executes only when the function is called.
Parameters and arguments

items: A parameter is the variable listed in the function definition.
An argument is the actual value passed when the function is called.

blocks.text: Here name is the parameter and "Sita" is the argument.
Returning a value
A function can send a value back to the caller with return. Use it when the caller needs the result, not just the side effect of printing it.

def add(x, y):
    return x + y

result = add(5, 3)
print("The sum is", result)

blocks.title: print() is not the same as return
blocks.text: A function that prints a result gives you nothing to calculate with. A function that returns a result lets the caller store it, compare it or pass it to another function. This distinction separates code that merely works from code that can be built on.
Scope of variables

items: A local variable is declared inside a function and can be used only there. It exists only while the function is running.
A global variable is declared outside every function and can be used throughout the program.

blocks.text:
x = 10          # global variable

def show():
    y = 5       # local variable
    print("x:", x)      # a function may read a global
    print("y:", y)

show()
# print(y)      # NameError - y does not exist outside show()
The commented-out last line is the point: y belongs to show(), and trying to use it elsewhere is an error.
Ways of passing arguments
1. Positional arguments
Matched to parameters by order.
2. Keyword arguments
Each argument is given with its parameter name, so order does not matter.
3. Default arguments
A parameter can have a default, used when no argument is supplied.

def power(base, exp=2):
    return base ** exp

print(power(4))       # uses the default: 4 ** 2 = 16
print(power(2, 3))    # overrides it:    2 ** 3 = 8
4. Variable number of arguments
When you do not know how many values will be passed, use *args, which collects them into a tuple.
Functions with and without return values

# Returns a value
def add(x, y):
    return x + y

# Does not return a value - it just does something
def show(message):
    print(message)

result = add(5, 3)
show("The sum is " + str(result))

Have students write a function that returns the area of a rectangle, then one that prints it, and ask which they could use inside a bigger calculation. That question lands the print/return distinction better than any explanation.

blocks.caption: User-defined function to get cube of a number

blocks.text: Program 1 — Factorial using a function

def factorial(n):
    result = 1
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        result = result * i
    return result

num = int(input("Enter a number: "))
print("Factorial of", num, "is", factorial(num))
Program 2 — Simple interest using a function

def simple_interest(principal, rate, time):
    interest = (principal * rate * time) / 100
    return interest

P = float(input("Enter Principal amount: "))
R = float(input("Enter Rate of interest: "))
T = float(input("Enter Time in years: "))

print("Simple interest =", simple_interest(P, R, T))
Program 3 — Area of a rectangle using a function

def area_rect(length, breadth):
    return length * breadth

l = float(input("Enter length: "))
b = float(input("Enter breadth: "))
print("Area of rectangle =", area_rect(l, b))
Program 4 — Largest of three numbers using a function
Program 5 — Area of a circle using a function

import math

def area_circle(r):
    return math.pi * r * r

radius = float(input("Enter radius: "))
print("Area of circle =", round(area_circle(radius), 2))
Using math.pi instead of writing 3.14 by hand is more accurate and makes the intention clearer.
Program 6 — A function with a default argument

def power(base, exp=2):
    return base ** exp

print("Square of 4:", power(4))
print("Cube of 2:", power(2, 3))

sections.title: Concept of Library and Packages in Python

blocks.text: A collection of pre-written code — modules and packages — that provides specific functionality you can use instead of writing it yourself.
For example, the math library helps with mathematical calculations, random generates random values, and pandas manages data in tables.
Using libraries saves time, reduces errors, lets you reuse code that has already been tested, and makes programs far more powerful than anything you could write alone.
A collection of related modules (Python files) arranged in folders.

blocks.title: Module versus library versus package
blocks.text: A module is a single Python file. A package is a folder of related modules. A library is the general term for reusable code you import — it may be one module or a collection of packages. Do not worry about the boundary; the exam asks for the general idea.
The four ways to import

import math
import random as rnd
from math import sqrt, pi

print(math.sqrt(16))        # 4.0
print(rnd.randint(1, 6))    # a random number from 1 to 6
print(pi)                   # 3.141592653589793

blocks.title: Prefer the first two styles
blocks.text: from math import * looks convenient but drops every name into your program at once, where it can quietly overwrite something else. Aliases such as pd, plt and np are the convention in real code and keep the source readable.
Standard libraries
Python ships with many standard libraries — they are available as soon as Python is installed, with nothing else to do. The ones in this chapter are:

head: Library
What it is for
Typical use
rows: Drawing shapes with a virtual pen
Working with tabular data and CSV files
blocks.caption: Libraries used in this chapter

blocks.text: Installing external packages
Some libraries, such as pandas and matplotlib, are not always present. Install them with pip from the terminal:

# In a terminal or command prompt
pip install matplotlib

# In Jupyter Notebook or Google Colab, prefix with !
!pip install matplotlib
Solved programs — using libraries
1. Area of a circle using the math library

import math

r = float(input("Radius: "))
area = math.pi * r * r
print(f"Area = {area:.2f}")
The :.2f inside the f-string formats the value to two decimal places.
2. Square root using the math library

import math

num = 16
print("Square root of", num, "is", math.sqrt(num))
3. Current date and time using datetime

import datetime

now = datetime.datetime.now()
print("Current date and time:", now)
print("Today's date:", now.date())
4. A random choice from a list

import random

colors = ["red", "green", "blue", "yellow"]
print("Random color:", random.choice(colors))
print("Random number from 1 to 6:", random.randint(1, 6))
5. Shuffling a list

import random

nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
random.shuffle(nums)
print("Shuffled list:", nums)

blocks.title: random.shuffle changes the list in place
blocks.text: It returns None and rearranges the list you passed in. Writing nums = random.shuffle(nums) therefore leaves nums as None — a mistake worth showing once.

blocks.caption: Concept of Library and Packages in Python

blocks.text: A Python module for drawing shapes and figures with simple commands, by moving a virtual pen — the "turtle" — around the screen.
It is a good way to learn geometry and to see what your loops are actually doing, because the picture is the output.

blocks.title: Turtle needs a real window
blocks.text: Turtle opens a graphical window, so it must be run on a computer with a display — it will not run in the embedded runner on this page, and it cannot run in a plain terminal. Use IDLE, PyCharm, Jupyter or Google Colab. Every program below is correct and is syntactically checked, but you need a Python installation to see the drawing.
Setting up

items: import turtle as t imports the module under the short name t.
t.speed() controls how fast the drawing happens.
t.shape() changes the cursor shape — the choices are turtle, arrow, circle, square, triangle and classic.

blocks.text: Movement commands

head: Command
What it does
rows: Moves straight to the position (x, y)
Lifts the pen, so moving draws nothing
Puts the pen back down, so moving draws again
blocks.caption: Turtle movement commands

blocks.text: Colour and filling

head: Command
What it does
rows: Sets the colour of the line
Sets the colour used to fill a shape
Starts recording a shape to fill
Fills the shape drawn since begin_fill()
Sets the thickness of the line
blocks.caption: Turtle colour commands

blocks.text:
import turtle as t

t.pencolor("navy")
t.fillcolor("gold")
t.begin_fill()
for _ in range(4):
    t.forward(100)
    t.right(90)
t.end_fill()
t.done()
Finishing the drawing

t.hideturtle()   # hides the turtle cursor (optional)
t.done()         # keeps the window open
t.done() tells Python the drawing is finished and that the window should stay open instead of closing the moment the program ends. Without it, the window may flash and disappear.
Solved programs — Turtle
1. A square

import turtle as t

t.speed(3)
for _ in range(4):
    t.forward(100)
    t.right(90)
t.done()
2. An equilateral triangle

import turtle as t

def triangle(side, color="pink"):
    t.fillcolor(color)
    t.begin_fill()
    for _ in range(3):
        t.forward(side)
        t.left(120)          # exterior angle of an equilateral triangle
    t.end_fill()

triangle(100)
t.done()
3. A filled circle and a polygon

import turtle as t

# Filled circle
t.fillcolor("orange")
t.begin_fill()
t.circle(60)
t.end_fill()

# A regular polygon with any number of sides
def polygon(sides, length, color="skyblue"):
    t.fillcolor(color)
    t.begin_fill()
    for _ in range(sides):
        t.forward(length)
        t.left(360 / sides)    # the turns must add up to 360
    t.end_fill()

polygon(6, 70)
t.done()

blocks.title: Why 360 / sides?
blocks.text: Walking right round a closed shape turns you through a full circle, 360 degrees. Each turn is therefore 360 divided by the number of sides. This one formula replaces a page of remembered angles and works for any regular polygon.
4. A star

import turtle as t

def star(side=120, color="violet"):
    t.fillcolor(color)
    t.begin_fill()
    for _ in range(5):
        t.forward(side)
        t.right(144)           # the star turning angle
    t.end_fill()

star(120)
t.done()
5. A filled square and triangle, using penup and pendown

import turtle as t

t.speed(4)
t.shape("turtle")
t.bgcolor("white")
t.pensize(2)

# A filled square
t.fillcolor("khaki")
t.begin_fill()
for _ in range(4):
    t.forward(120)
    t.right(90)
t.end_fill()

# Move without drawing, so the triangle sits beside the square
t.penup()
t.forward(180)
t.pendown()

# A filled triangle
t.fillcolor("salmon")
t.begin_fill()
for _ in range(3):
    t.forward(120)
    t.left(120)
t.end_fill()

t.hideturtle()
t.done()
6. A filled circle using a Turtle object

import turtle

t = turtle.Turtle()
t.color("blue")
t.fillcolor("lightblue")
t.begin_fill()
t.circle(50)
t.end_fill()
turtle.done()
7. Four filled circles in different colours

import turtle

t = turtle.Turtle()
t.speed(0)
colors = ["red", "blue", "green", "orange"]

for i in range(4):
    t.penup()
    t.goto(-150 + i * 100, 0)
    t.pendown()
    t.color(colors[i])
    t.fillcolor(colors[i])
    t.begin_fill()
    t.circle(40)
    t.end_fill()

t.hideturtle()
turtle.done()

The polygon formula (360 divided by the number of sides) is the payoff of this section — it turns five memorised shapes into one idea. Have students draw a pentagon, an octagon and a decagon without being told the angles.
A problem in a program that either stops it completely or makes it produce the wrong result.
Error handling exists so that a program can survive a runtime problem instead of crashing, and continue running smoothly.
The three types of error
1. Syntax error
The code breaks the rules of Python, so the program will not start at all. A missing colon, wrong indentation or a misspelled keyword are syntax errors.
2. Runtime error (exception)
The program starts but fails while running.

# print(10 / 0)        # ZeroDivisionError - division by zero
# int("abc")           # ValueError        - text that is not a number
# open("abc.txt")      # FileNotFoundError - no such file
3. Logical error
The program runs without crashing but gives the wrong answer, because the logic is wrong. These are the hardest to find, because Python reports nothing at all.

# Meant to find the average of 10, 20 and 30
a, b, c = 10, 20, 30
print("Wrong average:", a + b + c / 3)   # adds a and b before dividing
print("Right average:", (a + b + c) / 3)

blocks.title: The bracket that changes the answer
blocks.text: Division binds tighter than addition, so a + b + c / 3 means a + b + (c/3). Logical errors like this are why you should test a program with numbers whose answer you already know.
The try-except block

head: Block
When it runs
What it is for
rows: Only if an error occurs in try
Handles the error instead of crashing
Cleanup such as closing a file
blocks.caption: The four blocks

blocks.text: Why error handling matters

items: It prevents the program from crashing.
It handles input you did not expect from the user.
It makes the program more reliable.
It helps with debugging.
It allows resources to be cleaned up properly.
It gives the user a better experience.
It keeps large applications stable.

blocks.text: Solved programs — error handling
1. Squaring a number, with invalid input handled
2. Division with both division-by-zero and invalid input handled
Catching specific exceptions in order is better than catching everything, because each gets its own clear message.
3. Reading a file that may not exist
Using with closes the file automatically, whether or not an error occurred — so the finally block is not needed here.
4. A loop that keeps asking until the input is valid
Show the same program twice: once crashing with a traceback on bad input, once handled. Students who have seen a raw traceback once are far more willing to write try-except afterwards.
Variables hold data only while the program runs; when it ends, everything in memory is lost. File handling stores data permanently so it survives. It is needed to:

items: save user data for future use;
read existing data and analyse it;
record logs, reports and results automatically.

blocks.text: File handling modes

head: Mode
Meaning
Description
rows: Opens an existing file for reading only. Errors if the file does not exist
Opens a file for writing, and deletes any existing content
Opens a file and adds new data at the end
Opens a file for both reading and writing
Combined with another mode for images, audio and video
blocks.caption: File handling modes

blocks.title: "w" destroys what was there
blocks.text: Opening with "w" erases the existing contents before writing anything. If you want to keep what is there and add to it, use "a". This is the most damaging easy mistake in file handling, because the data is simply gone.
Writing and reading a text file

# Write text into a file
with open("hello.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Namaste, Nepal!\n")

# Read the text back
with open("hello.txt", "r") as f:
    content = f.read()
    print(content)
The with statement closes the file automatically when the block ends, even if an error occurs — so never leave a file open by accident.
Appending, and reading with "r+"

# Append: adds to the end without losing anything
with open("marks.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("Hari: 78\n")

# Read, then write
with open("info.txt", "r+") as f:
    print(f.read())
    f.write("\nThank you!")
Binary mode
Binary mode handles non-text data such as images, audio and video. Add b to the mode string, and the data is handled in bytes rather than characters.

with open("sample.bin", "wb") as f:
    f.write(b"PythonBinaryData")
Working with CSV files using pandas
A plain-text file that stores tabular data, with one record per line and the fields separated by commas.
pandas is the standard library for handling tabular data in Python. It stores a table in a structure called a DataFrame. It is worth using because it gives you:

items: Organised data — rows and columns that are easy to read and manipulate.
Cleaning and filtering — built-in functions for missing values, duplicates and filtering.
Speed — it handles large data sets quickly, and works well alongside matplotlib and NumPy.

blocks.text: Solved programs — files and pandas
1. Write student marks to a text file

with open("marks.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Sita: 75\n")
    f.write("Ram: 80\n")

print("Marks saved successfully.")
2. Read and display a text file

with open("marks.txt", "r") as f:
    print(f.read())
3. Append to a text file

with open("marks.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("Hari: 78\n")

print("New marks added.")
4. Count the lines in a text file

with open("marks.txt", "r") as f:
    lines = f.readlines()

print("Total students:", len(lines))
5. Create a DataFrame of students and marks

import pandas as pd

data = {"Name": ["Asha", "Bimal", "Deepak"], "Marks": [85, 90, 78]}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)
print(df)
6. Create and save a CSV file

import pandas as pd

data = {"Name": ["Sita", "Ram"], "Marks": [85, 90]}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)          # create the table
df.to_csv("students.csv", index=False)   # save it as CSV
print("Saved to students.csv")
index=False stops pandas writing the row numbers as an extra column — you almost always want it.
7. Read and display a CSV file

import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("students.csv")
print(df)
8. Add a Grade column based on marks

import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("students.csv")
df["Grade"] = ["A" if m >= 80 else "B" for m in df["Marks"]]
print(df)
9. Append a new row to an existing CSV

import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("students.csv")
new_row = pd.DataFrame([{"Name": "Deepak", "Marks": 85}])
df = pd.concat([df, new_row], ignore_index=True)
df.to_csv("students.csv", index=False)
print("New record appended to students.csv")
10. Handle missing values

import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("students.csv")
df = df.fillna(0)      # replace every missing value (NaN) with 0
print(df)

short.q: What is the difference between for and while loops?
short.a:
A for loop is used when you know in advance how many times the body should run — it steps over a sequence such as range(1, 6) or a list. A while loop is used when you do not know the number of repetitions in advance and instead repeat until a condition becomes false.

The practical difference: for i in range(5) runs exactly five times, whereas while i <= 5 runs as long as the condition holds, which means you must make sure something inside the loop eventually changes it — otherwise it never ends.

short.q: Write one use of comments in Python.
short.a:
Comments explain what a piece of code does and why, so that someone reading it later — including you, months afterwards — can follow the reasoning without working it out from the code alone.

They are also useful for temporarily disabling a line while testing, and for describing what a function expects and returns.

short.q: What is a function?
short.a:
A function is a named block of organised, reusable code that performs one specific task. It is defined with the def keyword and runs only when it is called.

Functions let you write a piece of logic once and use it many times instead of copying it, which makes programs shorter, easier to read and far easier to change. They can accept data through parameters and send a result back with return.

short.q: What is the use of t.penup() in Turtle?
short.a:
t.penup() lifts the pen so that moving the turtle does not draw a line.

It is used to reposition the turtle before starting a new shape. You call t.penup(), move to the new position with t.goto() or t.forward(), then call t.pendown() to start drawing again. Without it, moving to a new starting point would drag a stray line across the drawing.

short.q: What is the purpose of t.done() in Turtle programs?
short.a:
t.done() tells Python that the drawing is finished and that the window should stay open instead of closing as soon as the program ends.

Without it the window may flash briefly and disappear before you can see the result. It is normally the last line of a Turtle program.

short.q: What is the use of the Matplotlib library in Python?
short.a:
Matplotlib is used to create charts and graphs from data — line charts, bar charts, pie charts, scatter plots and more.

It turns numbers into pictures so that trends and comparisons can be seen at a glance instead of read from a table. In practice you import it as import matplotlib.pyplot as plt and finish with plt.show() to display the chart.

short.q: Write one use of the finally block in Python.
short.a:
The finally block holds code that runs no matter what — whether an exception occurred or not — so it is used for cleanup such as closing a file or releasing a connection.

For example, if you open a file inside try, closing it in finally guarantees it is closed even when reading raised an error.

short.q: What is a CSV file?
short.a:
A CSV (Comma Separated Values) file is a plain-text file that stores tabular data: one record per line, with the fields separated by commas.

It is a simple, widely supported way to move a table between programs. Pandas reads one with pd.read_csv() and writes one with df.to_csv().

short.q: Write one advantage of using Pandas.
short.a:
Pandas organises data into rows and columns — a DataFrame — so that a whole table can be filtered, sorted, summarised and cleaned with a single line of code instead of hand-written loops.

It also handles the awkward cases for you: missing values (fillna), duplicates, reading and writing CSV files, and large data sets efficiently.

short.q: Mention any two types of charts supported by Matplotlib.
short.a:
Line chart — shows a trend over time, drawn with plt.plot().

Bar chart — compares categories, drawn with plt.bar().

A pie chart is the third common type, drawn with plt.pie(), and shows how a whole divides into proportions.

long.q: Explain the different data types in Python with examples.
long.a:
Python works out the type of a value from the value itself, so you do not declare types. The types used in this course are:

TypeHoldsExample
strText"Hello"
intWhole number10
floatDecimal number3.14
boolTrue or FalseTrue
listOrdered collection, changeable[62, 75, 80]
tupleOrdered collection, unchangeable("Sita", 15)
dictKey-value pairs{"name": "Sita", "class": 10}

The distinctions that matter in practice. List versus tuple: a list can be changed after creation, a tuple cannot, so use a tuple for a fixed group such as a name and an age. int versus float: dividing with / always produces a float, even when the result is whole. And str is what input() always returns, which is why numbers read from the user must be converted before arithmetic.

long.q: Write and explain a Python program using if-elif-else to classify marks into "Distinction", "First Division", and "Pass".
long.a:
marks = int(input("Enter your marks: "))

if marks >= 80:
    print("Distinction")
elif marks >= 60:
    print("First Division")
elif marks >= 40:
    print("Pass")
else:
    print("Fail")

How it works. Python tests the conditions from top to bottom and runs the first one that is true, so once a branch is taken the rest are skipped. That ordering is what makes the chain work: a mark of 85 is also greater than 60 and greater than 40, but the first test catches it, so it is correctly reported as Distinction.

This is why the conditions must be written from the narrowest to the broadest. Reversed, testing marks >= 40 first, every student would be classified as "Pass", including those with 95.

The final else catches everything that fell through, which here means a mark below 40.

long.q: What is a user-defined function? Explain parameters, arguments, and return values with suitable code examples.
long.a:
A user-defined function is a function the programmer writes, as opposed to the built-in functions Python provides. It is defined with the def keyword and runs only when called.

def area_rect(length, breadth):   # length, breadth are PARAMETERS
    return length * breadth

print(area_rect(10, 5))              # 10, 5 are ARGUMENTS

Parameters are the variables named in the function definition, the placeholders. Arguments are the actual values supplied when the function is called. In the example, length and breadth are parameters; 10 and 5 are arguments.

Return values. return sends a result back to the caller so it can be stored and used in further work:

def add(x, y):
    return x + y

result = add(5, 3)         # result is 8
print(result + 2)          # 10 - we can carry on using the value

The important contrast is with print(), which only displays a value and gives the caller nothing to work with. A function that returns can be composed into larger programs; one that merely prints cannot.

long.q: Explain local and global variables with an example program.
long.a:
The scope of a variable is the part of the program where it can be used.

A local variable is created inside a function and can be used only within that function; it exists only while the function is running. A global variable is created outside every function and can be used throughout the program.

x = 10          # global variable

def show():
    y = 5       # local variable
    print("x:", x)      # a function may READ a global
    print("y:", y)

show()
print("x outside:", x)
# print(y)      # NameError - y does not exist out here

The commented-out line is the whole point: y belongs to show(), and referring to it outside the function raises a NameError. Local variables keep functions self-contained, so two functions can each use a variable named y without interfering with one another.

long.q: What is the difference between a library and a package? Explain with examples of standard libraries like math and random.
long.a:
A module is a single Python file. A package is a folder containing related modules. A library is the general term for a body of reusable code that you import: it may be a single module or a collection of packages.

So the difference is one of scale and structure. A package is a specific way of organising modules, while "library" describes what the code is for, namely being reused.

math is a standard library providing mathematical functions:

import math
print(math.sqrt(81))    # 9.0
print(math.pi)          # 3.141592653589793

random is a standard library for generating random values:

import random
print(random.randint(1, 6))                       # whole number 1 to 6
print(random.choice(["red", "green", "blue"]))    # a random item

Both are standard libraries, meaning they are installed with Python and need nothing extra. Libraries such as pandas and matplotlib are external and must be installed with pip first.

long.q: Describe Turtle graphics in Python.
long.a:
Turtle graphics is a Python module for drawing shapes by moving a virtual pen, the "turtle", around the screen. It is part of the standard library and is widely used to teach programming, because the output is a picture you can see immediately.

import turtle as t

t.speed(3)
t.pencolor("navy")
t.fillcolor("gold")

t.begin_fill()
for _ in range(4):
    t.forward(100)
    t.right(90)
t.end_fill()

t.hideturtle()
t.done()

The main groups of commands:

  • Movement - forward(), backward(), left(), right(), goto().
  • Pen control - penup() and pendown() to move without drawing, pensize() for thickness.
  • Colour - pencolor(), fillcolor(), wrapped by begin_fill() and end_fill().
  • Shapes and setup - circle(), shape(), speed(), bgcolor().
  • Finishing - hideturtle() and done(), the latter keeping the window open.

The most useful idea is that a regular polygon with n sides turns 360 / n degrees at each corner, because the turns must add up to a full circle. That single formula draws any regular polygon.

Turtle opens a graphical window, so it must be run on a computer with a display, in IDLE, PyCharm, Jupyter or Google Colab.

long.q: What are exceptions? Explain the role of try, except, else, and finally blocks with an example.
long.a:
An exception is a runtime error, a problem that appears while the program is running, such as dividing by zero, converting text that is not a number, or opening a file that does not exist. If it is not handled the program stops and shows a traceback.

try:
    n = int(input("Enter a number: "))
    result = 100 / n
except ValueError:
    print("That was not a valid number.")
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print("Cannot divide by zero.")
else:
    print("Result:", result)
finally:
    print("Done.")

The four blocks:

  • try - the code that might fail. It is always attempted first.
  • except - runs only if a matching error occurred. This is where the error is handled instead of ending the program. You can have several, one per exception type.
  • else - runs only if the try block succeeded. Keeping it separate from try makes clear which line you expect to fail.
  • finally - runs no matter what, whether there was an error or not. It is used for cleanup such as closing a file.

Listing specific exception types, as above, is better than catching everything: each problem gets its own clear message, and unrelated bugs are not silently swallowed.

long.q: What are the different file modes used in Python? Write short code examples for "read", "write", and "append" modes.
long.a:
ModeMeaningDescription
"r"ReadOpens an existing file for reading only; errors if it is not there
"w"WriteOpens for writing and deletes any existing content
"a"AppendOpens and adds new data at the end
"r+"Read and writeOpens for both
"b"BinaryCombined with another mode for images, audio and video

Read:

with open("marks.txt", "r") as f:
    print(f.read())

Write - note that this replaces whatever was there:

with open("marks.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Sita: 75\n")

Append - keeps what is there and adds to it:

with open("marks.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("Hari: 78\n")

Using with closes the file automatically at the end of the block, even if an error occurred, so files are never left open by accident.

long.q: Write a program using Pandas to read, filter, and add a new column to a CSV file, and explain each step.
long.a:
import pandas as pd

# 1. Read the CSV file into a DataFrame
df = pd.read_csv("students.csv")
print("All students:")
print(df)

# 2. Filter: keep only students with 80 marks or more
top = df[df["Marks"] >= 80]
print("\nStudents with 80 or more:")
print(top)

# 3. Add a new column, worked out from the marks
df["Grade"] = ["A" if m >= 80 else "B" for m in df["Marks"]]
print("\nWith the new Grade column:")
print(df)

# 4. Save the result
df.to_csv("updated_students.csv", index=False)

Step by step.

Read. pd.read_csv() turns the file into a DataFrame, a table with named columns and numbered rows.

Filter. df[df["Marks"] >= 80] builds a True/False mask for every row and keeps only the True ones. This single expression replaces a whole loop.

Add a column. Assigning to df["Grade"] creates the column; the list comprehension produces one value per row.

Save. to_csv() writes it back out. index=False leaves out the row numbers, which would otherwise become a pointless extra column.

long.q: Explain data visualization with Matplotlib. Write programs to create (a) a line chart, (b) a bar chart, and (c) a pie chart, and explain the purpose of each.
long.a:
Data visualization is representing data with charts and graphs so that patterns are visible at a glance. It makes information simpler and faster to understand, reveals trends and comparisons, and communicates results far better than a table of raw numbers.

(a) Line chart - for trends over time.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

months = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May"]
sales = [100, 120, 90, 150, 180]

plt.plot(months, sales, marker="o")
plt.title("Monthly Sales")
plt.xlabel("Months")
plt.ylabel("Sales")
plt.show()

The connected points make the direction of change obvious: you can see the dip in March and the rise afterwards without reading a single number.

(b) Bar chart - for comparing categories.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

subjects = ["Math", "Science", "English", "Nepali"]
marks = [78, 85, 72, 80]

plt.bar(subjects, marks, color="green")
plt.title("Marks by Subject")
plt.xlabel("Subject")
plt.ylabel("Marks")
plt.ylim(0, 100)
plt.show()

Bar heights are easy to compare side by side, which is exactly what you want when the categories have no natural order.

(c) Pie chart - for parts of a whole.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

labels = ["Food", "Rent", "Transport", "Others"]
values = [40, 30, 20, 10]

plt.pie(values, labels=labels, autopct="%1.1f%%", startangle=90)
plt.title("Monthly Expenses")
plt.axis("equal")
plt.show()

Each slice shows a share of one total, so a pie chart answers "how is the whole divided?". autopct prints the percentage on each slice, and axis("equal") keeps the circle round.

In every case plt.show() is what actually displays the chart: everything before it only builds it.

practical.q: Activity 5 - Default and variable arguments.
practical.a:
A default argument is used when the caller omits it; *args collects any number of arguments into a tuple.

# Function with a default argument
def power(base, exp=2):
    return base ** exp

print("Square of 4:", power(4))
print("Cube of 2:", power(2, 3))

# Function with a variable number of arguments
def total(*nums):
    return sum(nums)

print("Total of 1, 2, 3, 4 =", total(1, 2, 3, 4))

import math, random

practical.q: Activity 8 - Building a house from shapes.
practical.a:
Compose a rectangle, a triangle, a door and a window using functions, positioning the parts with penup(), pendown() and goto().

import turtle as t

def rectangle(w, h, color):
    t.fillcolor(color)
    t.begin_fill()
    for _ in range(2):
        t.forward(w)
        t.left(90)
        t.forward(h)
        t.left(90)
    t.end_fill()

def triangle(side, color):
    t.fillcolor(color)
    t.begin_fill()
    for _ in range(3):
        t.forward(side)
        t.left(120)
    t.end_fill()

t.speed(5)

# Body of the house
t.penup(); t.goto(-100, -100); t.pendown()
rectangle(200, 150, "wheat")

# Roof
t.penup(); t.goto(-120, 50); t.pendown()
triangle(240, "brown")

# Door
t.penup(); t.goto(-25, -100); t.pendown()
rectangle(50, 80, "sienna")

# Window
t.penup(); t.goto(50, -20); t.pendown()
rectangle(50, 50, "lightblue")

t.hideturtle()
t.done()

blocks.text: We use smart technologies every day without thinking about how they work. When a mobile phone camera focuses on faces by itself, when YouTube suggests a video we might like, or when Google Maps shows the fastest route, the computer is doing something that looks intelligent. An email application moves unwanted messages into the spam folder without being told to, and Google Translate turns a Nepali sentence into English in an instant.
These abilities are usually associated with human intelligence. When machines are built to carry out such tasks, the technology behind them is called Artificial Intelligence (AI).

This chapter covers AI and machine learning, AI in robotics, generative AI tools and how to use them responsibly, the ethics of AI, the Internet of Things, extended reality, cloud computing, and e-commerce, e-governance and e-education.

blocks.title: A distinction worth making early
blocks.text: Humans think naturally and emotionally; machines make decisions from data and rules. AI can beat a human at chess and still have no idea what chess is. Keeping that gap in view prevents both over-trust and dismissal.
The branch of computer science concerned with creating machines or software that can think, learn and make decisions in ways that resemble human intelligence.
However, humans think naturally and emotionally, while machines make decisions from data and rules. AI simulates intelligent behaviour; it does not feel it.
Areas that make up AI

items: Machine learning — systems that improve from data rather than from explicit instructions.
Natural language processing — understanding and producing human language.
Computer vision — interpreting images and video, such as a camera recognising a face.
Robotics — machines that sense and act in the physical world.
Expert systems — programs that encode specialist knowledge to give advice.
Neural networks — systems loosely modelled on the brain, and the basis of modern deep learning.
Speech recognition — converting spoken language into text, as used by voice assistants and call-centre automation.
Knowledge representation and reasoning — storing knowledge so that a machine can reason logically; rule-based systems and decision-making applications are examples.
Planning and decision making — deciding what action to take and when, such as route planning and scheduling systems.

blocks.text: Applications of AI

items: Healthcare — analysing scans, suggesting diagnoses, speeding up drug discovery.
Education — personalised learning, automated marking, translation.
Transport — route planning, traffic prediction, self-driving vehicles.
Business and finance — fraud detection, recommendations, forecasting.
Communication — spam filtering, voice assistants, real-time translation.

blocks.text: Ask students to list every place they met AI on the way to school — face unlock, a recommendation feed, a spam filter, a map. The list is always longer than they expect, and it makes the topic concrete before any definition is given.

Suppose a computer is shown thousands of photographs, each labelled "cat" or "dog". The more examples it studies, the better it understands the relationships and the common trends that separate the two. From this we can see that computers can learn from past data and make better decisions over time, just as people learn from experience.
The ability of a computer to learn from examples and past data rather than being given explicit instructions for every case.
In machine learning, computers learn in a way similar to humans, by gaining experience from past examples.
How machine learning works

blocks.title: Training a system to tell a cat from a dog
items: Collect data — gather many photographs of cats and dogs.
Prepare the data — label each photograph, and clean and organise the set.
Find patterns — the system analyses the data and learns useful features, such as shapes or colours.
Test and improve — the trained system is tested with pictures it has never seen. When it makes mistakes, it adjusts and improves its learning.
Make predictions — finally, when a new picture is given, the system predicts whether it is a cat or a dog.

blocks.text: Key terms in AI and ML

head: Term
Meaning
rows: The information the computer learns from, such as photographs or records
The program produced by training, which makes the predictions
The process of feeding data to the system so it can learn
The output the model produces for new input
The measurable properties the system learns from, such as shape or colour
How often the model is right
blocks.caption: Key terms in AI and ML

blocks.text: Supervised learning

A type of machine learning in which the computer is trained using labelled data — data where every example already carries the correct answer. The computer learns from these examples and later uses that knowledge to make predictions for new data.

blocks.title: The supervised learning process
items: Collect labelled data — every example comes with its correct answer.
Split the data — part for training, part for testing, so the model can be checked on data it has not seen.
Choose an algorithm — select the learning method to use.
Train the model — the algorithm learns the relationship between inputs and outputs by minimising errors; it compares its predicted output with the actual output.
Evaluate the model — the trained model is tested using unseen data, and accuracy and error rate are measured.
Make predictions — once trained, the model predicts outputs for new input data.
Email spam detection — the system learns from emails already marked "spam" or "not spam".
Medical diagnosis — trained on scans that doctors have already labelled.

blocks.text: Unsupervised learning
A type of machine learning in which the computer is trained using unlabelled data and must find patterns or groupings by itself.

blocks.title: The unsupervised learning process
items: Collect unlabelled data — the dataset contains only input data, with no labels or correct answers.
Feed the data to the algorithm — the system is given the data without any guidance about what to look for.
Find patterns and groupings — the algorithm finds structure, such as clusters of similar customers.
Interpret the results — a person examines the groups found and decides what they mean.
Customer segmentation — grouping shoppers by buying behaviour without being told what the groups are.
Anomaly detection — spotting unusual patterns, such as fraudulent transactions.

head: Basis
Supervised learning
Unsupervised learning
rows: Trained using data that already includes the correct answers or labels
Trained using data without any labels; must find patterns on its own
To predict specific outcomes based on known examples
To discover hidden patterns or groupings in the data
Higher — someone must label the data first
Lower — the data needs no labelling
blocks.caption: Supervised versus unsupervised learning

blocks.title: The labelling is the expensive part
blocks.text: The reason supervised learning is not used everywhere is that someone has to label the training data by hand — often thousands of examples. Unsupervised learning skips that step, at the cost of less predictable results.

We often see machines that move and work automatically. A robotic vacuum cleaner cleans the floor by itself, factory robots assemble products, and robots are sent into space to explore planets. These machines move, sense their surroundings and perform tasks without constant human control.
A machine designed to perform work automatically — one that can sense its surroundings, decide what to do and act on that decision.
The basic operating cycle
Robots generally follow four main steps while working:
Sense → Think → Act → Repeat

items: Sense — collect information from the environment using sensors.
Think — process the collected data and make decisions using AI or programmed logic.
Act — perform the required task or movement using motors or actuators.
Repeat — continuously repeat the cycle to complete the assigned task efficiently.

blocks.text: How AI helps robots
1. Perception
AI lets a robot understand what its sensors detect — recognising objects, obstacles and people rather than merely recording raw values.
2. Planning
AI works out the sequence of actions needed to reach a goal, such as the route a vacuum cleaner should take round a room.
3. Learning
Robots improve with experience, adjusting their behaviour as conditions change rather than repeating a fixed routine.
4. Communicating and coordinating
A robot uses AI to communicate with humans or with other robots, to share information and coordinate actions. This allows several robots to work together on large or complex tasks.
In a warehouse, several robots communicate to organise deliveries without colliding or repeating work.
5. Adapting and staying safe
AI allows robots to sense changes in their environment and adjust their actions for safety — stopping when a person steps into their path, for instance.
Simulation of simple robotic tasks
Simple robots use the same basic principle of Sense → Think → Act → Repeat. Common examples are:

items: Line-following robot — uses sensors to detect a black line on the floor and adjusts its wheels to stay on it while moving. It is commonly used in factories to transport materials between workstations.
Obstacle-avoiding robot — detects an object in its path and turns to avoid it.
Light-following robot — moves towards the brightest source of light.

blocks.text: A free online robot simulator lets students run the Sense-Think-Act loop without any hardware, which is the point of the practical activity for this section. Two students can compare how different sensor placements change the result.

Students today can ask a computer to explain a science topic, help write an essay outline, create a poster design, or even generate an image from a short sentence. A student may ask a tool to explain photosynthesis, summarise a chapter, or design a presentation slide. From these examples we can see that computers are not only answering questions — they are creating new content such as text, images and ideas.
Artificial intelligence that produces new content — text, images, code, audio or video — rather than only analysing or sorting what already exists.
Popular generative AI tools
1. ChatGPT

An advanced AI tool developed by OpenAI. It can create human-like text responses and hold meaningful conversations, answering questions, writing essays, summarising information and solving problems across subjects.
It can help explain a science topic, draft a paragraph, or assist in understanding a difficult concept.
2. Microsoft Copilot
Microsoft’s AI assistant, built into Windows, Word, Excel, PowerPoint and Teams, which drafts text, summarises documents and answers questions about your own files.
3. Other widely used tools

items: Google Gemini — Google’s assistant, integrated with Search, Docs and Gmail.
Claude — an assistant from Anthropic, oriented towards long documents and careful reasoning.
Image generators — tools such as DALL·E, Midjourney and Stable Diffusion, which create pictures from a written description.

blocks.text: Using generative AI for learning
Generative AI can be a useful learning companion when used responsibly. It helps with writing, problem-solving and creative projects.
For writing

items: Explain photosynthesis in simple terms.
Help me write an essay outline about climate change.
Create five quiz questions about the history of Nepal.

blocks.text: For problem solving

items: Solve this maths problem step by step.
Explain the logic behind this program and where it goes wrong.

blocks.text: For creative projects

items: Suggest a poster design for a science exhibition.
Help me draft a script for a short class presentation.

blocks.text: Disadvantages of generative AI tools

items: May produce incorrect information — AI can give wrong or incomplete answers, and it presents them confidently.
Lacks human judgement — it cannot truly understand emotions, values or moral decisions.
Can reduce original thinking — relying too heavily on AI may limit creativity and independent effort.
Requires internet access — most tools need an online connection to work.

blocks.title: The failure mode that matters most
blocks.text: Generative AI states wrong answers in exactly the same confident tone as right ones. The skill to teach is not how to use the tool but how to check it: ask for a source, test it against something you already know, and never submit output you could not explain.

The most commonly used AI-powered productivity platforms are Google Workspace and Microsoft 365. Both now include AI features that do part of the work for you — drafting text, summarising documents, cleaning up audio and organising email.
A. Google Workspace
A cloud-based productivity and collaboration suite developed by Google. It lets individuals, teams and organisations create, communicate and collaborate online efficiently.
Google Workspace — formerly known as G Suite — includes Google Docs, Gmail, Google Drive, Google Meet and more.
1. Google Docs

A cloud-based word processing application, similar to Microsoft Word but working entirely online. It allows users to create, edit and share documents from any device with internet access. AI in Google Docs assists users in writing, editing and improving content.
When writing an essay, Google Docs can suggest better sentence structures and correct spelling automatically.

items: Smart Compose — suggests how to finish a sentence as you type.
Grammar and spelling checks — corrected automatically as you write.
Help me write — drafts a first version from a description.
Voice typing — turns speech into text.

blocks.text: 2. Gmail
Google’s email service. AI in Gmail reduces the effort of dealing with a busy inbox.

items: Smart Reply — suggests short replies you can send in one tap.
Spam filtering — moves unwanted mail out of the inbox automatically.
Priority inbox — sorts mail by what seems most important.

blocks.text: 3. Google Drive
Cloud storage for files of any kind, with AI search that can find documents by describing their contents and even read text inside images.
4. Google Meet

A video conferencing and online meeting tool. It allows people to host or join virtual meetings, classes or webinars from anywhere using the internet. AI in Google Meet enhances online learning and communication.

items: Noise cancellation — removes background sounds during calls.
Auto captioning — displays live subtitles for accessibility.
Framing — keeps the speaker well positioned in the video.

blocks.text: B. Microsoft 365
Microsoft 365 is Microsoft’s equivalent suite, with AI built into Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Teams through Copilot.
1. Microsoft Word
A word processing application used to create, edit, format and print documents, widely used in offices, schools and homes. AI in Word helps improve writing accuracy and clarity.
Students can use Word’s Editor to correct grammar errors, or the Read Aloud tool to hear an essay before submitting it.

items: Editor — checks grammar, spelling and style.
Read Aloud — reads the document back, which makes errors easier to hear than to see.
Copilot — drafts and rewrites passages.

blocks.text: 2. Microsoft Excel
A spreadsheet application. AI in Excel removes much of the manual work of analysing data.

items: Suggested charts — recommends a suitable chart for the selected data.
Pattern recognition — spots trends and outliers.
Natural language questions — lets you ask about the data in plain language instead of writing formulas.

blocks.text: 3. Microsoft PowerPoint
Presentation software. AI in PowerPoint helps both with the look of the slides and with the delivery.

items: Designer — suggests layouts and designs for a slide.
Presenter Coach — gives real-time feedback on speaking pace and tone during a rehearsal.
Live Captions — shows subtitles during a presentation, which also helps non-native speakers.

blocks.text: 4. Microsoft Outlook
Email and personal information management software, widely used for email communication, scheduling and organisation. AI in Outlook improves email and schedule management.
Outlook helps students remember assignment submission dates or meeting times.

items: Focused Inbox — separates important mail from everything else.
Suggested replies — offers quick responses.
Schedule suggestions — proposes meeting times that suit everyone.

blocks.text: 5. Microsoft Teams
A collaboration platform combining chat, meetings and file sharing. AI provides meeting transcripts, summaries and action points, so nobody has to take notes by hand.
Why this matters for students

items: Speed — routine work such as formatting, spelling and summarising is partly automated, leaving more time for the thinking.
Collaboration — real-time sharing and editing of files among classmates; teachers can comment and give feedback directly in documents.
Version history — students can track and restore earlier work, which makes experimenting safe.

blocks.text: Have students write the same paragraph twice — once unaided, once with the AI features on — and then compare. The lesson is not that AI writes better, but that it writes faster and still needs checking: ask them to find one wrong suggestion in the AI version.

People today use AI systems for studying, working, creating and making decisions that affect their lives. As AI becomes more powerful, using it responsibly matters more. The three concerns that come up most are bias, privacy and security.
1. AI bias
Systematic and unfair discrimination in an AI system. It occurs when the system makes unfair or incorrect decisions because of biased data, design or algorithms.
Since AI learns from human-created data, any inequality present in that data can lead to biased results.

If an AI system is designed to grade essays, it should be trained using examples from different schools, languages and writing styles to ensure fairness. Trained on only one kind of writing, it would mark down perfectly good essays that simply sound different.
Reducing bias

items: Use training data that genuinely represents everyone affected.
Test the system on different groups and check the results match.
Keep a human reviewing decisions that affect people significantly.
Be open about how the system was built and what data it used.

blocks.text: 2. Privacy in AI

Privacy means protecting personal information — what is collected about you, who can see it and what it is used for. AI systems often need a great deal of data, and that creates risk: information shared with a tool may be stored, analysed or used to train future systems.
Typing a friend’s address or a classmate’s medical detail into an online AI tool may put that information somewhere it cannot be recalled from.
Protecting privacy

items: Use strong passwords and avoid sharing sensitive information — the single most effective habit.
Share only what the task genuinely needs.
Check what a tool does with your data before you use it.
Do not enter other people’s personal information without their knowledge.

blocks.text: 3. Security in AI
Security means protecting AI systems against cyber threats. Two common threats are:

items: Data poisoning — deliberately corrupting the training data so the system learns the wrong thing.
Adversarial attacks — inputs crafted to fool a system, such as an image altered so that a classifier misreads it.
Phishing and impersonation — AI-generated messages and voices used to deceive people.

blocks.text: Improving security

items: Keep software and systems up to date.
Verify requests through a second channel before acting on them.
Limit what data a system can reach.
Monitor systems for unusual behaviour.

blocks.text: Why ethics matters

items: AI decisions affect real people — who gets a job, a loan or a place.
Unfair systems are hard to detect, because they look neutral.
Trust, once lost, is very hard to rebuild.
Students are already using these tools, so the habits formed now carry forward.

blocks.title: Responsible use for students, in one sentence
blocks.text: Use AI to help you think, not to think for you: check what it produces, never present its work as your own, and never hand it anyone else’s personal information.

sections.title: Concept of Internet of Things (IoT) and its Applications

blocks.text: Today many devices around us work automatically. A smart light turns on when it gets dark, a fitness band counts steps and heart rate, and a refrigerator can alert us when food is about to expire. These devices can be controlled using a mobile phone or computer, often from anywhere.
A network of physical objects — appliances, vehicles, wearable devices and machines — that contain sensors and software and can exchange data with each other and with people over the Internet.

These "smart" objects can communicate with each other and with people through smartphones, tablets or computers. By combining sensors, software and Internet connectivity, IoT makes devices more intelligent, interactive and useful in daily life.
A smart light bulb connects to your home Wi-Fi network. You can control it from your phone even when you are not at home.
How an IoT system works

head: Component
What it does
Example
rows: Collect data from the physical world
A temperature sensor in a room
Cloud software compares the reading to your setting
Lets the user see and control the system
A phone app showing the temperature
blocks.caption: The four components of an IoT system

blocks.text: Applications of IoT
1. Smart homes

IoT devices make homes intelligent and automated — smart lights that turn on and off automatically, thermostats that adjust room temperature, and refrigerators that alert users when food is about to expire. Security cameras, doorbells and smart locks add safety.
2. Wearables
Fitness bands and smartwatches record steps, heart rate and sleep, and share the data with a phone app.
3. Healthcare

IoT improves patient care and monitoring. Wearable fitness trackers record heart rate, sleep and physical activity; smart pills confirm whether patients have taken their medicine; and remote monitoring systems let doctors observe patients’ conditions from home.
4. Smart cities

IoT helps cities become cleaner, safer and more efficient. Traffic lights adjust their timing based on real traffic, waste bins signal when they are full, and street lighting dims when nobody is around.
5. Agriculture and industry
Soil sensors trigger irrigation only when needed, and factory machines report wear before they break down, so maintenance happens before failure.
Advantages of IoT

items: Convenience and accessibility — devices can be controlled remotely from anywhere, and routine tasks such as switching on lights can be automated, saving time and effort.
Efficiency — resources such as electricity and water are used only when needed.
Safety — monitoring and alerts catch problems early.
Better decisions — real data replaces guesswork.

blocks.text: Disadvantages and risks

items: Privacy concerns — connected devices collect a great deal of personal data.
Security risks — every connected device is a possible way in for an attacker.
Cost — devices and installation can be expensive.
Complexity — systems from different makers do not always work together.
Reliability risks — interruptions in Internet or power affect performance. If a smart home system loses its Internet connection, security cameras or alarms may stop working, creating safety risks.

sections.title: Concept of Extended Reality (XR) and Virtual Reality (VR)

blocks.text: The collective term for all immersive technologies, including Virtual Reality (VR), Augmented Reality (AR) and Mixed Reality (MR). It covers any system that extends, enhances or blends the real and virtual worlds to create realistic, interactive experiences.
XR lets users move seamlessly between different forms of digital immersion — from simple AR overlays to fully simulated VR worlds.
1. Virtual Reality (VR)
A fully digital environment that replaces what the user sees, usually experienced through a headset. The user is immersed in a simulated world rather than the real one.

blocks.title: How VR works
items: Creation of a virtual environment — a virtual world is built using computer graphics, 3D modelling and simulation software. It may look like a game world, a classroom, a hospital or any imaginary place.
Input from the user — the user wears a VR headset and may use controllers, gloves or sensors. These detect head movement, hand movement and body position.
Processing and rendering — the computer redraws the scene continuously to match the user’s movements.
Display and feedback — the headset shows the updated scene, and audio and haptic feedback complete the experience.

blocks.text: Advantages of VR

items: It provides an engaging and realistic environment for learning and training.
It allows users to explore places and situations that are otherwise difficult or dangerous to reach.
It offers a safe space for practising real-world skills and operations.
It makes education and entertainment more interactive, improving focus and understanding.

blocks.text: 2. Augmented Reality (AR)
Technology that overlays digital content onto the real world, usually seen through a phone camera or AR glasses. The real environment stays visible and is added to.
A camera app that shows how a piece of furniture would look in your room before you buy it.
3. Mixed Reality (MR)
Technology in which real and virtual objects interact with each other. Virtual objects behave as though they truly exist in the user’s environment.
Wearing MR glasses, a user can place a virtual object on a real table and move it with their hands.

1. Education
Students can visit ancient cities, explore the solar system or examine a human heart in three dimensions instead of reading about them.
2. Training and professional development

XR provides realistic simulations for skill-based learning. Medical students can perform virtual surgeries, pilots can practise flying in flight simulators, and engineers can design and test machines in 3D before real production. Emergency responders can train for natural disasters or rescue missions without facing real risks.
3. Entertainment
XR offers new ways to experience games, films and live events.
Challenges of XR

items: The equipment and software can be expensive, and not easily available to everyone.
It requires powerful computers, high-quality graphics and stable internet connections to run smoothly.
Prolonged use may cause health issues such as eye strain, headaches or motion sickness.

sections.title: Concept of Cloud Computing and its Applications

blocks.text: Using computer services such as data storage, software applications and processing power over the Internet, instead of keeping them on your own computer.

It is called the cloud because these services are available online and can be reached from anywhere — much as clouds in the sky are everywhere. Cloud computing has transformed how individuals and organisations store, access and process information.

blocks.title: Someone else’s computer
blocks.text: A useful honest description of the cloud: it is a computer in someone else’s building that you reach over the Internet. The files are real files on a real disk — which is precisely why the service provider matters.
Types of cloud services — the service models
1. Software as a Service (SaaS)
Ready-to-use software applications available through a web browser. Users do not install or update anything.
Gmail, Google Docs, Microsoft 365 online.
Typically used by end users — anyone who wants the application without managing it.
2. Platform as a Service (PaaS)
A platform on which developers can build, test and run their own applications without managing the servers underneath.
Google App Engine, Heroku.
Typically used by developers.
3. Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)
Virtual servers, storage and networking provided over the Internet. The user manages the operating system and applications; the provider manages the hardware.
Amazon Web Services EC2, Microsoft Azure Virtual Machines.
Typically used by IT administrators and system architects.

blocks.text: Types of clouds — the deployment models

items: Public cloud — services available to anyone over the Internet, run by a provider. Example: Google Drive.
Private cloud — used by a single organisation, often on its own servers, for greater control. Example: a bank’s internal cloud.
Hybrid cloud — a mix of the two: ordinary work in the public cloud, sensitive data kept privately.

blocks.text: Depending on data sensitivity and resource needs, organisations choose the model that suits secure and efficient operations.
Applications of cloud computing

items: Google Workspace for Education — Google Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive and Classroom. Students can write assignments, analyse data, create presentations and submit work from anywhere.
Storage and backup — photos, documents and automatic backups kept safely off the device.
Streaming — video and music delivered without storing the files locally.
Collaboration — several people editing one document at the same time.

blocks.text: Advantages

items: Accessible from anywhere with an internet connection.
No large upfront cost for hardware.
Storage and capacity can grow as needed.
Files are backed up and recoverable if a device fails.
Software updates happen automatically.

blocks.text: Disadvantages

items: An internet connection is essential — without one, nothing works.
Data is held by a third party, which raises privacy questions.
Ongoing subscription costs can add up.
Outages at the provider stop everything.
