short.q: Write any two applications of Artificial Intelligence in daily life.
short.a:
Spam filtering in email — the mail application learns from messages you have marked as spam and moves similar ones out of your inbox automatically, without being given a fixed rule for every case.

Recommendations on video and shopping sites — the system studies what you have watched or bought and suggests what you might want next.

Other everyday examples are face recognition when unlocking a phone, voice assistants, live translation, and route planning that avoids traffic.

short.q: What is supervised Learning? Give one example.
short.a:
Supervised learning is a type of machine learning in which the computer is trained using labelled data — data in which every example already carries the correct answer. The system learns the relationship between the inputs and those answers, and then uses it to make predictions for data it has not seen before.

Example: email spam detection. The system is given thousands of emails already marked "spam" or "not spam". From these it learns what spam looks like, and afterwards it classifies new mail on its own.

short.q: Define Robotics and mention fields that contribute to it.
short.a:
Robotics is the branch of technology concerned with designing, building and operating robots — machines that can sense their surroundings, decide what to do and perform work automatically without constant human control.

It draws on several fields: mechanical engineering for the body and movement; electronics and electrical engineering for motors, sensors and control circuits; computer science and artificial intelligence for perception, planning and decision-making; and, depending on the task, control engineering and materials science.

short.q: How does Artificial Intelligence help robots in decision-making and safety?
short.a:
A robot follows the cycle Sense → Think → Act → Repeat. AI is what makes the "think" step real.

Decision-making. AI lets the robot interpret what its sensors detect — recognising an object or a person rather than just recording numbers — plan a sequence of actions to reach a goal, and improve with experience instead of repeating a fixed routine. It also lets several robots communicate and coordinate so they do not collide or duplicate work.

Safety. AI allows the robot to sense changes in its environment and adjust: stopping when a person steps into its path, slowing on a slippery surface, or selecting a different route when an obstacle appears.

short.q: Write any two rules or best practices that students should follow when using AI tools responsibly.
short.a:
Check the output before you trust it. Generative AI states wrong answers in exactly the same confident tone as right ones, so treat every answer as a first draft to verify — test it against something you already know, and ask for a source.

Never submit AI work as your own. Use it to explain, to outline or to check your thinking; the writing you hand in should be yours, and you should be able to explain every line of it.

A third worth adding: never enter anyone else’s personal information into an AI tool.

short.q: Define the Internet of Things (IoT) in simple words and give daily-life examples.
short.a:
The Internet of Things is a network of everyday objects — appliances, vehicles, watches, machines — that contain sensors and software and can send and receive data over the Internet. In plain terms, it is ordinary things made able to talk to each other and to you.

Examples. A smart bulb that connects to your Wi-Fi and can be switched on from your phone when you are not at home; a fitness band that counts steps and heart rate and syncs the data to an app; and a refrigerator that alerts you when food is about to expire.

short.q: Write any two benefits of using AI in productivity applications for students.
short.a:
Speed on routine work. Spelling, grammar, formatting, summarising and slide layout are partly automated, so more of the time goes into the thinking that actually matters.

Better collaboration. Real-time sharing and editing mean classmates can work on one document together, teachers can comment directly in the file, and version history lets a student restore earlier work — which makes it safe to experiment.

short.q: Mention applications of Virtual Reality (VR) in education or training, with a brief note on how VR helps in learning.
short.a:
Applications. Medical students performing virtual surgery; pilots practising in flight simulators; engineering students assembling and testing a machine in 3D; and classes visiting places they could not otherwise reach, from ancient cities to the inside of a human heart.

How it helps. VR gives a safe place to practise real skills — mistakes cost nothing and can be repeated — and it lets students experience things that are too distant, too small, too dangerous or simply impossible to visit. Learning by doing, in a space where failure is free, is more engaging and better retained than reading about it.

short.q: State two benefits and challenges of XR technologies.
short.a:
Benefits. XR makes learning and training engaging and realistic, and it allows people to explore places and situations that would otherwise be difficult or dangerous to reach — medical students can operate, and emergency responders can rehearse for disasters, without any real risk.

Challenges. The equipment and software are expensive and not available to everyone, and the systems need powerful computers, good graphics and a stable internet connection. Prolonged use can also cause eye strain, headaches or motion sickness.

short.a:

One benefit. Learning can happen from anywhere and at any time, and a lesson can be revisited as often as a student needs — which means material reaches places that do not have enough teachers, and nobody is left behind by the pace of a single class.

long.q: Explain what Machine Learning (ML) is and describe the steps involved in how it works. Give one example from daily life.
long.a:
Machine Learning is the ability of a computer to learn from examples and past data instead of being given an explicit instruction for every case. Rather than a programmer writing rules — "if it has pointed ears, it is a cat" — the system studies many examples and works the rules out for itself. It is a branch of artificial intelligence.

The steps, using the cat-or-dog example:

  1. Collect data — gather many photographs of cats and dogs.
  2. Prepare the data — label each photograph, then clean and organise the set.
  3. Find patterns — the system analyses the data and learns useful features, such as shapes or colours.
  4. Test and improve — the trained system is tested with pictures it has never seen. When it makes mistakes, it adjusts and improves its learning.
  5. Make predictions — when a new picture arrives, the system predicts whether it shows a cat or a dog.

A daily-life example. Email spam detection. The system is given thousands of messages already marked "spam" or "not spam", learns what distinguishes them, and then classifies new mail by itself — getting better the more mail it sees. Video recommendations work the same way: the more you watch, the better the suggestions fit.

long.q: Describe the working process and examples of Supervised and Unsupervised Learning. Compare them on the basis of data type, objective, and human involvement.
long.a:
Supervised learning. The computer is trained using labelled data, where every example already carries the correct answer. The process is: collect labelled data; split it into a training set and a test set; choose an algorithm; train the model, which learns the relationship between inputs and outputs by minimising errors — comparing its predicted output with the actual one; evaluate the model on unseen data, measuring accuracy and error rate; then make predictions for new input.

Examples: email spam detection, where the system learns from mail already marked spam or not spam; and medical diagnosis, trained on scans that doctors have already labelled.

Unsupervised learning. The computer is given unlabelled data and must find the structure by itself. The process is: collect unlabelled data; feed it to the algorithm; let the algorithm find patterns and groupings, such as clusters of similar customers; then have a person interpret what the groups mean.

Examples: customer segmentation, grouping shoppers by buying behaviour without anyone defining the groups in advance; and anomaly detection, spotting an unusual transaction that may be fraud.

Human involvementHigher — someone must label the data first, which is slow and expensiveLower — no labelling needed, but a person must interpret the results

long.q: Explain the five main ways AI helps robots (Perception, Planning, Learning, Communication, and Adaptation) with suitable examples.
long.a:
A robot runs the cycle Sense → Think → Act → Repeat. AI is what gives substance to each stage.

1. Perception. AI lets the robot understand what its sensors detect, rather than merely recording raw values — recognising an object, an obstacle or a person. Example: a robot vacuum cleaner distinguishing a chair leg from a wall, and a factory robot identifying which part is on the belt.

2. Planning. AI works out the sequence of actions that will reach a goal. Example: deciding the order in which to cover the rooms of a house, or the route a warehouse robot should take to fetch an item.

3. Learning. The robot improves with experience, adjusting behaviour as conditions change instead of repeating a fixed routine. Example: a robot that learns which route through a room is quickest at different times of day.

4. Communication. AI enables a robot to exchange information with people or with other robots and coordinate actions. Example: in a warehouse, several robots share their positions so they organise deliveries without colliding or duplicating work.

5. Adaptation. AI lets the robot sense changes in its surroundings and adjust for safety and effectiveness. Example: stopping when a person steps into its path, slowing on a wet floor, or choosing another route when a door is shut. This is what makes a robot safe to work beside people rather than behind a cage.

long.q: Explain what Generative AI is, list any three popular Generative AI tools, and describe one limitation and one responsible-use practice for students.
long.a:
Generative AI is artificial intelligence that creates new content — text, images, code, audio or video — rather than only analysing or sorting what already exists. A student might ask it to explain photosynthesis, summarise a chapter, outline an essay or design a slide, and get something new back each time.

Three popular tools.

  1. ChatGPT — developed by OpenAI; produces human-like text, answers questions, writes essays, summarises information and solves problems across subjects.
  2. Microsoft Copilot — built into Windows, Word, Excel, PowerPoint and Teams; drafts text, summarises documents and answers questions about your own files.
  3. Google Gemini — Google’s assistant, integrated with Search, Docs and Gmail.

Image generators such as DALL·E, Midjourney and Stable Diffusion do the same for pictures, creating an image from a written description.

One limitation. It may produce incorrect or incomplete information — and crucially, it presents wrong answers in exactly the same confident tone as right ones, so the reader has no warning. It also lacks human judgement: it cannot genuinely understand emotions, values or moral questions.

One responsible-use practice. Check before you trust, and never pass off its work as your own. Use it to explain, outline or test your thinking, then verify the result against a source or something you already know — and make sure you could explain every line you submit.

long.q: Describe how AI is used in Microsoft 365 applications such as Word, Excel, and Teams, with examples.
long.a:
Microsoft 365 includes AI through Copilot and through features built into each application.

Word. AI helps improve writing accuracy and clarity. The Editor checks grammar, spelling and style; Read Aloud reads the document back, which makes awkward phrasing easier to hear than to see; and Copilot can draft or rewrite a passage. Example: a student runs the Editor over an essay to correct grammar, then uses Read Aloud to hear how it flows.

Excel. AI removes much of the manual work of analysing data. It suggests charts suited to the selected figures, recognises patterns such as trends and outliers, and lets you ask questions in plain language instead of writing formulas. Example: selecting a table of monthly sales and asking which month grew fastest, without constructing a formula.

Teams. AI supports meetings by producing transcripts, summaries and action points, so nobody has to take notes by hand. Example: after a group meeting, each member receives the decisions and the tasks assigned to them.

Across all three, the pattern is the same: the AI handles the mechanical work — correcting, formatting, summarising, calculating — so that people spend their time on the judgement.

long.q: Explain the three main ethical concerns in AI — Bias, Privacy, and Security — with examples and ways to reduce or manage each.
long.a:
1. Bias. AI bias is systematic and unfair discrimination arising from biased data, design or algorithms. Because AI learns from data created by people, any inequality in that data produces biased results. Example: a recruitment system trained mainly on one group’s résumés learns to favour that group. An essay-marking system trained on writing from only one kind of school would mark down good essays that sound different.

Reducing it: use training data that genuinely represents everyone affected; test the system on different groups and compare results; keep a human reviewing decisions that affect people significantly; and be open about how the system was built.

2. Privacy. Privacy is about protecting personal information — what is collected, who sees it and what it is used for. AI systems need large amounts of data, which creates risk: information typed into a tool may be stored or used to train future systems. Example: entering a classmate’s address or medical detail into an online AI tool may put it somewhere it can never be recalled from.

Protecting it: use strong passwords and avoid sharing sensitive information; share only what the task genuinely needs; check what a tool does with your data before using it; and never enter other people’s personal information without their knowledge.

3. Security. Security means protecting AI systems against cyber threats. Examples: data poisoning, where training data is deliberately corrupted so the system learns the wrong thing; adversarial attacks, where an input is crafted to fool a classifier; and AI-generated phishing or voice impersonation used to deceive people.

Managing it: keep software up to date; verify unusual requests through a second channel before acting; limit what data a system can reach; and monitor systems for abnormal behaviour.

long.q: Explain the working of an IoT system using its four basic components (Sensors, Connectivity, Data Processing, User Interface). Illustrate with a clear step-by-step example (e.g., smart irrigation or smart light).
long.a:
The four components.

  1. Sensors and devices — collect data from the physical world: temperature, light, motion, heart rate.
  2. Connectivity — carries that data onward, using Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, a mobile network or a dedicated protocol.
  3. Data processing — software, often in the cloud, analyses the readings and decides what should happen.
  4. User interface — an app or dashboard lets the user see what is happening and change the settings.

Worked example — smart irrigation.

Step 1, sense. A soil-moisture sensor buried in a field measures how wet the soil is and reports a value, say 20 per cent.

Step 2, connect. The sensor sends that reading over Wi-Fi or a low-power network to the cloud.

Step 3, process. The cloud software compares 20 per cent with the threshold the farmer set, say 40 per cent. It is below the threshold, and the weather forecast shows no rain, so it decides to water.

Step 4, act. The system switches the valve on. When the sensor later reports 45 per cent, it switches the valve off.

Step 5, interface. The farmer’s phone shows the current moisture level, a log of when watering happened, and a control to override the system.

The result is water used only when the soil actually needs it, controlled from anywhere — and, as the same chapter notes, the corresponding risk is that a lost internet connection or a power cut can leave the system unable to act.

long.q: Compare VR, AR, and MR in terms of immersion and interaction with the real world. Provide one example use-case for each and mention one advantage and one limitation for any one of them.
long.a:
TypeWhat the user seesImmersionInteraction with the real worldExample use-case
VRA fully simulated world; the real one is hiddenTotal — the user is placed inside the digital worldNone; the user is cut off from itA medical student practising surgery in a simulated operating theatre
ARThe real world with digital content laid over itPartial — the real world stays the main viewDigital content is added, but does not respond to real objectsA phone app showing how a sofa would look in your room
MRReal and virtual objects togetherPartial to high — digital objects behave as though presentReal and virtual objects interact with each otherPlacing a virtual machine part on a real workbench and assembling it by hand

VR — one advantage and one limitation.

Advantage: it offers a safe space for practising real-world skills. Mistakes cost nothing and can be repeated as often as needed, and students can experience places that are too distant, too small or too dangerous to visit — pilots rehearse emergencies in a flight simulator with no risk at all.

Limitation: prolonged use can cause eye strain, headaches or motion sickness, and the equipment is expensive and needs powerful hardware plus a stable internet connection.

long.q: Explain the three service models—SaaS, PaaS, and IaaS—with one clear example each, and state who typically uses each model.
long.a:
The three service models describe how much of the computing stack the provider looks after and how much you do.

1. Software as a Service (SaaS). A finished application delivered through a web browser. You do not install or update anything — you simply use it. Example: Gmail, or Google Docs. Typical users: end users — anyone who wants the application without managing it.

2. Platform as a Service (PaaS). A platform on which developers build, test and run their own applications, without managing the servers underneath. Example: Google App Engine, or Heroku. Typical users: developers, who want to write code rather than maintain infrastructure.

3. Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS). Virtual servers, storage and networking delivered over the Internet. The provider looks after the hardware; you manage the operating system, the applications and the data. Example: Amazon Web Services EC2, or Microsoft Azure Virtual Machines. Typical users: IT administrators and system architects.

ModelYou getYou manageTypical user
SaaSA finished applicationOnly your data and settingsEnd users
PaaSA platform to build onYour applications and dataDevelopers
IaaSServers, storage, networkOperating system, applications, dataIT administrators

A simple way to remember it: with SaaS you rent the finished product, with PaaS you rent the workshop, and with IaaS you rent the building.

long.q: Compare e-Commerce, e-Governance, and e-Education by stating for each: (a) purpose, (b) one example/service, (c) one benefit, (d) one challenge.
long.a:
e-Commercee-Governancee-Education
(a) PurposeBuying and selling goods and services over the InternetDelivering government services and information electronically, and improving transparencyDelivering education and training through digital technology
(b) ExampleOnline shopping sites; selling used items on hamrobazar.comApplying for a passport or paying tax onlineLive classes on a video platform; Google Classroom; Khan Academy
(c) BenefitShop at any hour from anywhere, with far wider choice and easy price comparisonNo queueing or travel, and services available outside office hoursLearn from anywhere and revisit a lesson as often as needed
(d) ChallengeYou cannot inspect goods before buying; risk of fraud and delivery problemsThe digital divide — rural areas may lack internet — plus cyber risk and limited computer literacyNeeds a device, a reliable connection and considerable self-discipline

What they have in common. All three move an activity that once required physical presence — visiting a shop, a government office, a classroom — onto the Internet. Each brings convenience and reach, and each replaces one barrier with another: the queue is gone, but a reliable connection and some digital skill are now required.

practical.q: Activity 1 — AI-based robotics simulation.
practical.a: To understand how robots use AI to sense, decide and perform tasks automatically. You need a computer or smartphone with internet access and any free online robot simulator. Set the robot a task, such as following a line, and observe the Sense → Think → Act → Repeat cycle. Change one thing — the sensor position, the speed — and compare the result.

practical.q: Activity 2 — Explore a generative AI tool.
practical.a: Ask a generative AI tool to explain a topic you are studying, then check its answer against your textbook. Note anything it got wrong or left out. This builds the habit of verifying output rather than trusting it.

practical.q: Activity 3 — Use an AI writing feature.
practical.a: Write a short paragraph in Google Docs or Microsoft Word with the AI suggestions switched on. Compare it with a paragraph you wrote unaided, and list one suggestion you rejected and why.

practical.q: Activity 4 — Spot the bias.
practical.a: Think of an AI system that makes decisions about people — marking essays, filtering job applications. List who might be treated unfairly if the training data came from only one group, and what data would fix it.

practical.q: Activity 5 — Privacy audit.
practical.a: Look at one app you use daily and find out what data it collects. Write down three pieces of personal information you would never type into an AI tool, and say why.

practical.q: Activity 6 — Map an IoT system.
practical.a: Choose a smart device you have seen — a smart bulb, a fitness band. Identify its four components: what it senses, how it connects, where the data is processed, and how the user sees and controls it.

practical.q: Activity 7 — IoT risks.
practical.a: For the device in Activity 6, list two things that go wrong if the internet connection fails, and one privacy risk from the data it collects.

practical.q: Activity 8 — VR, AR or MR in your subject.
practical.a: Choose a topic you find hard to visualise. Describe how VR, AR and MR would each present it, and say which would work best and why.

practical.q: Activity 9 — Classify cloud services.
practical.a: List five online services you use — mail, storage, video, documents — and classify each as SaaS, PaaS or IaaS. Explain one classification to a classmate.

practical.q: Activity 10 — Public, private or hybrid.
practical.a: A school keeps public brochures in Google Drive but student records on its own server. Name this model and explain why the school made that choice.

practical.q: Activity 11 — An e-commerce purchase, end to end.
practical.a: Write out the six stages of buying something online, from browsing to review, and note which model (B2C, B2B, C2C or C2B) each example belongs to.

practical.q: Activity 12 — Compare the three "e"s.
practical.a: Make a table comparing e-Commerce, e-Governance and e-Education by purpose, one example, one benefit and one challenge. Add one service from Nepal for each.

quick_revision.title: Artificial intelligence
points: AI creates machines that can think, learn and decide like humans — but from data and rules, not from feeling.
Its areas include machine learning, natural language processing, computer vision, robotics, expert systems, neural networks, speech recognition, knowledge representation, and planning.

quick_revision.title: Machine learning
points: ML learns from examples instead of following explicit instructions.
The steps: collect data, prepare it, find patterns, test and improve, make predictions.
Supervised uses labelled data to predict an outcome; unsupervised uses unlabelled data to find hidden groupings.
Labelling data by hand is what makes supervised learning expensive.

quick_revision.title: Robotics
points: A robot senses, thinks, acts and repeats.
AI gives it perception, planning, learning, communication and adaptation.
Adaptation — stopping for a person, choosing another route — is what makes a robot safe to work beside people.

quick_revision.title: Generative AI and productivity tools
points: Generative AI creates new text, images, code, audio or video.
Tools include ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini and image generators.
It can be wrong and says so in the same confident tone as when it is right — always check.
In Google Docs, Smart Compose finishes sentences; in PowerPoint, Presenter Coach comments on pace and tone.

quick_revision.title: Ethics in AI
points: Bias is systematic unfairness from biased data, design or algorithms; use representative data and keep a human reviewing significant decisions.
Privacy means protecting personal information — share only what the task needs, and never enter other people’s details.
Security threats include data poisoning, adversarial attacks and AI-generated phishing; keep software updated and verify unusual requests.

quick_revision.title: Internet of Things
points: IoT is a network of physical objects that exchange data over the Internet.
Four components: sensors, connectivity, data processing, user interface.
Applications: smart homes, wearables, healthcare, smart cities, agriculture and industry.
Risks: privacy, security, cost, complexity, and reliability — a lost connection can disable alarms and cameras.

quick_revision.title: Extended reality
points: XR is the umbrella term for VR, AR and MR.
VR replaces the real world; AR overlays it; MR lets real and virtual objects interact.
Used in education, training and entertainment.
Challenges: expensive equipment, powerful hardware needed, and eye strain or motion sickness with prolonged use.

quick_revision.title: Cloud computing
points: Cloud computing uses storage, applications and processing power over the Internet.
Service models: SaaS (finished app, for end users), PaaS (platform, for developers), IaaS (infrastructure, for IT administrators).
Deployment models: public, private and hybrid.
Advantages: anywhere access, no hardware cost, easy growth, automatic updates. Disadvantages: needs the internet, data held by a third party, subscription cost.

quick_revision.title: e-Commerce, e-Governance, e-Education
points: e-Commerce buys and sells: browse, add to cart, checkout, pay, deliver, review. Models: B2C, B2B, C2C, C2B.
e-Governance delivers government services: G2C, G2B, G2G, G2E. Challenges include the digital divide.
e-Education delivers learning online — flexible and repeatable, but it needs a device, a connection and self-discipline.

detailed.title: AI and Contemporary Technologies
detailed.overview: This chapter covers the technologies shaping computing today: artificial intelligence and machine learning, AI in robotics, generative AI tools and how to use them responsibly, the ethics of AI, the Internet of Things, extended reality, cloud computing, and e-commerce, e-governance and e-education. Each topic is explained with its underlying idea, its applications, and its limitations — because knowing what a technology cannot do is as important as knowing what it can.
